speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
On the orders of the day:
Hon. ROBERT W. MAYHEW (Minister of Fisheries): I wish to refer, Mr. Speaker, to a matter of significant importance to the salmon fishing and processing industry of British Columbia.
It will be recalled that the government has been concerned since last fall with the situation facing the salmon, canning industry in 1948, as a result of the withdrawal of export controls on certain species of salmon. To give effect to the representations of the fishermen, eo-operaltives, and eanners, the government announced, on April 8, that effective as of that date British Columbia fishermen would be permitted to export, without restriction, raw spring salmon-export of fresh cohoe salmon was also permitted, buit only up to September 1 of this year-and that fresh sockeyes, pinks and chums would be retained in Canada for processing.
It was indicated at the time that the policy of the government sought to retain for processing in Canada those species of salmon normally canned and that the plan was a compromise between the different interests; further, that the plan indicated flexibility in [DOT]the event of changing conditions.
From information received during the past few weeks from the Pacific coast, it appears evident there is a distinct possibility that large quantities of sockeyes, pinks and chums will be frozen and exported, thus defeating the original plan. This would have had the effect of depriving the canning industry in British Columbia of considerable quantities of raw' material, which would result in curtailed operations and loss of direct employment in the canneries, and indirectly cause loss to many ancillary industries.
In view of these changed conditions it has been found desirable and necessary for the government to extend its policy of affording safeguards to both fishermen and management in the salmon canning industry of British Columbia. Accordingly, an amendment has been made to order in council, P.C. 1521, effective immediately, that sockeyes, pinks and chums in a frozen condition will not be permitted to be exported. However, after September 1 of this year frozen chums may be exported.
The combination of the two plans will, I am informed, be quite acceptable to both the fishermen and the operators in British Columbia. It will have the effect of giving additional

Inquiries of the Ministry
force to the submissions of the fishermen, cooperatives and operators, namely the retention in Canada for processing of species of salmon which normally are canned. At the same time, the normal export trade in fresh spring and cohoe salmon will be unchanged; likewise in the case of frozen cohoes and fall-caught chums after September 1, the normal past itrade will not be interfered with.

My hon. friend asks whether there is any substantial loosening of the control over activities on the Lord's day. In Nova Scotia there is, in addition to the Lord's Day Act, the preconfederation statute to which I have referred.

speechtext:
I sought to take part in the debate a few minutes ago in an endeavour to answer one or two questions which had been raised. The hon. member for Lake Centre raised the question whether the imperial act of 1781 is in effect in Ontario. The Ontario courts ruled in 1880 that it was in effect in the province. I refer to the case of Rex v. Barnes. 1880. 45 Upper Canada Queen's Bench reports, 276. where that question was raised, and the court determined that the imperial act of 1781 was in effect in the province of Ontario.

The Lord's Drey Act
I need not weary the committee by reviewing all the stages by which that came about, but it goes back to proclamations of the eighteenth century. The English law as of October 15, 1792, was adopted as the law of Ontario except as repealed, altered, varied, modified, or affected by any act of the imperial parliament still having the force of law in Ontario or any act of the late province of Upper Canada or of the province of Canada or of the province of Ontario si ill having the force of law in Ontario. That is the law of Ontario today, as set out in the Ontario statutes. Historically the laws of England, civil and criminal, were supposed to be introduced into Canada by royal proclamation of October 7. 1763. The criminal law was not displaced by the Quebec Act of 1774, 14 Geo. Ill chapter S3, but was continued in the province of Upper Canada. The legislature of the province, by the act of 1792, 32 George III. chapter 1. provided that in matters of property and civil rights the laws of England should prevail. In 1800. apparently for greater caution, the act 40 George III. chapter 1 (Upper Canada) provided that "the criminal law of England as it stood on the 17th day of September. 1792". should be the criminal law of the province. The date September 17. 1792. was the date of the first of the legislature in that year; and, according to the existing law, the statutes of the session took effect as of the first day of the session.
That is how this old act of 1781 came to be part of the law of Upper Canada, and that was not changed by the Constitutional Act of 1841. When confederation became effective, no right was reserved to the new provincial legislature to modify the old pre-confederation law.
The hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario raised the question whether this is a matter of substance or not. I think a word might be said further on that. The fact is that the legislature of Ontario some years after confederation sought to pass legislation on the subject of Sunday observance. That legislation incidentally is in many respects comparable in terms to the old imperial legislation. This act to which I am referring was enacted in the reign of Queen Victoria, and it was carried forward into the Revised Statutes of Ontario, -1897, chapter 246.
The test of the jurisdiction of the provinces went to the privy council in the year 1903 in the case of the Attorney General of Ontario v. the city of Hamilton Street Railway, 1903 Appeal Cases, pages 524. The privy council determined that the provincial legislatures had no power to pass such legislation, holding
that the law with respect to Sunday observance falls within the jurisdiction of parliament to legislate in respect of the criminal law; and consequently, the legislature of the province of Ontario has had no general jurisdiction over Sunday observance except in so far as scope is given to the legislatures of the provinces by the federal statute, the Lord's Day Act.
The statute that is now being amended is the Lord's Day Act. chapter 123 of the Revised .Statutes' of Canada. 1927, In taking the step that is involved in section 2, it does not seem to me that anything is being done that need give any member of the house reason for pause. The principal law of this country with reference to Sunday observance is today, and will continue to be under the bill before us, the federal statute, the Lord's Day Act. For more than a generation the enforcement of the act has been left by federal legislation in the hands of the attorneys general of the provinces.
Having regard to the fact that there is considerable divergence of usage in the matter of Sunday observance in different parts of Canada, I do not see what serious objection should be raised to the principle of section 16 of this act, that enforcement should be left largely i,n the hands of the provinces. The attorneys general of the provinces, as the chief law enforcement officers, are the persons, in my opinion, best qualified to take responsibility in matters of enforcement of the Lord's Day Act. In enacting this present bill it seems to me that we are not displacing any substantive law that is vital today. We are simply removing legislation that would not be enforced today by any attorney general in any province. We are bringing our laws in some measure up to date.

The result of the amendment would be merely to add the word "dietitian". There are in Canada some 650 trained dietitians who are united in an organization called the Canadian Dietetic Association. Two or three weeks ago they met in Montreal and passed certain resolutions, and it was unanimously requested that they be excluded from the operation of this act along with those other professional people mentioned. I do not wish to misinterpret or give incorrect information as to what the reasons were for refusal by the committee on industrial relations; but if I am correct, it was largely because if dietitians were brought into the section the committee felt they would also have to include nurses. Rather than carry that idea into effect, they decided not to include dietitians.
The dietitians wrote to the committee on industrial relations on May 17 of this year. I have in my hand a copy of their letter, and I should like to read merely the opening and closing paragraphs. The opening paragraph reads as follows:
The Canadian Dietetic Association strongly urges that dietitians should be included with those other professional groups such as the medical, dental, architectural, engineering and legal professions, the members of which are excluded from the definition or "employees" under the terms of paragraph 1, section 2 (i) 2 of Bill No. 195 presently under consideration by your committee and this for the reasons hereinafter set forth.
Then they set forth a number of reasons and the concluding paragraph reads:
For the foregoing reasons, the Canadian Dietetic Association submits that your committee should accede to the present request and amend Bill No. 195 so as to establish clearly that dietitians are excluded from the operation of the act as is the ease with members of other professions whose training requirements and the scope of whose work are on a similar level.
The reason submitted by the committee was,
I understand, a purely negative one. Had this been the United States of America, where similar legislation operates under the Taft-Hartley Act, the request would have received a positive interpretation. I have before me a synopsis of U.S. 3020, which is from the

Industrial Relations
Taft-Hartley Act, and I should like to quote these positive reasons:
Term "professional employee" means (S2 12):
(a)	any employee engaged in work.
(i)	predominantly intellectual and varied in character as opposed to routine, mental, manual, mechanical or physical work;
(ii)	involving the consistent exercise of discretion and judgment in its performance.
(iii)	of such a character that the output produced or the result accomplished cannot be standardized in relation to a given period of time;
(iv)	requiring knowledge of an advanced type in a field of science or learning customarily acquired by a prolonged course of specialized intellectual instruction and study in an institute of higher learning or a hospital, as distinguished from a general academic education or from an apprenticeship or from training in the performance of routine mental, manual or physical processes; or
(b)	any employee, who:
_ (i) has completed the courses of specialized intellectual instruction and study prescribed in clause fiv) of paragraph (a), and
(ii) is performing related work under the supervision of a professional person to qualify himself to become a professional employee as defined in paragraph (a).
I maintain that if this proposed amendment carries it will not prejudice the position of any of those who wish to be included in this section, or of those who desire not to be included. As an organization, the dietitians maintain that they are professional people. They had a certain dignity which they wish to have recognized, and they are anxious to be placed in a position where they may command the respect of other professional people. For these reasons, and especially because of the positive request which they make, which in my opinion would not prejudice any professional group, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Prince:
That section 2, subsection 1, paragraph (i), subparagraph (ii) be amended by inserting the word "dietitian" immediately after the word "medical."

There was general agreement on the definition of "employee" prior to its going to the committee. I have expressed this opinion before. We have had a great deal of difficulty with the language of this section. Wherever it has been drafted there has always been difficulty. In human institutions you have to place a measure of trust in the people whom you appoint to a board. I am convinced of this, and I know that my legal friends will agree with me. Where you have a board made up of individuals such as we have, and as they have in several provinces, representative of industry and labour, with an impartial chairman, the conclusion reached was that this was about the best language that could be used in the circumstances. There has been no serious objection to it. If we attempted to draft a bill which included what everyone wanted it would be a poor looking document.
So far as I know we have had no difficulty in the national board, nor do I know of any serious difficulties in the provincial boards. They have decided who was an employee within the meaning of P.C. 1003. After the study we gave the matter I am convinced that no serious difficulty would arise in connection with the definition of "employee."

Perhaps I might give an example. On the railways are section foremen who have been members of trade unions for the last fifty years. The conductor on a train has complete control, because he has charge of the train. He takes and gives orders. Then, in a small industry you may find someone who is called a foreman, and whose position would be the equivalent of a superintendent or executive in a larger industry. The only rule one can lay down is the rule of common sense as applied to the industry concerned. The language must be broad enough to enable it to be properly interpreted by men of intelligence. I know we have such men on the national board, and I can say we also have them on the provincial boards. In the light of the language of the section I am prepared to accept their judgment in the matter.

I think the matter is of sufficient importance that at least some of the pertinent points should be brought out. I am not going to repeat what was said by the hon. member for Bow River, because I agree with everything he has said.
I would point out that there is nothing compulsory in the bill. If it applied to doctors, lawyers, engineer's and what have you, the first thing they would have to do would be to conform with the mechanics of the bill, form a tradie union, get certification and all the rest of it. If they did not want to do that, there is nothing in the bill that compels them to.
There are two classifications of engineers. There is the engineer who is an employee, and there is the engineer at the managerial level. In effect the one is the boss of the other. My understanding of the representations that were made for the exclusion of engineers from this bill is that they were made by those at the managerial level. During the war engineers were permitted to form collective bargaining organizations under P.C. 1003 and come within the scope of that legislation.
As the hon. member for Bow River suggested, there are 1,100 employee engineers who have formed collective bargaining organizations and now have collective bargaining agreements with their employers. If we exclude engineers from this legislation we wipe out the bargaining rights of 1,100 people who have said that they want them because they have made collective bargaining agreements under P.C. 1003, which is being replaced by this legislation.
We hear a lot about democracy. I think the employee engineer has as much right to form a unit of his own under the provisions of this bill and to bargain with the employer as the managerial engineer has to say that he does not. want to come under it. If he does not want to come under it there is nothing to compel him to come under it unless he goes through the mechanics provided by' the bill and forms a collective bargaining organization.
I do not think this house or the committee has the right to say to employee engineers who want the same rights as are given to others under this legislation that they must not continue the arrangements they made under P.C. 1003 and' have been working under for the past six or seven years. We have no right to exclude them from this bill, and thus wipe out the agreements they have entered into which have improved their conditions.

I suggest that the minister give serious consideration to the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Vancouver East and restore democracy to these 1,100 engineers who are already within the scope of the present legislation. They should be permitted to continue. If the remaining strata of the engineering profession want to continue as they are, if they want to keep their professional units outside the scope of this legislation, that is their right. They do not have to come in, but I do not think we have the right to exclude employee engineers who have already shown a desire to come under the legislation. It is too serious a step to take to exclude them now.

Mr. Chairman, I gather that the amendment, coming from a private member, will give us an opportunity to have a free vote on this resolution. I am glad to know as a matter of fact that the committee will have that opportunity, but there are a great number of hon. members here who were not on the committee, and perhaps those of us who were there will give a few words of explanation.
The clause as read by the chairman is what is commonly known as the voluntary revocable check-off. It means nothing more than that the employer collects union dues, which the employee voluntarily asks him to do, the employee having the right to revoke it at any time he likes. There is no hardship on the employer. It does not interfere with any of the rights of the employer, be they managerial or otherwise, nor does it interfere with any of the rights that belong to the general public. It is a voluntary act on the part of the employee, and all it requires is a mechanical act by someone in the office to check it off in the same way that all office staffs now collect income tax deductions, unemployment insurance deductions, perhaps deductions for Red Cross and even for payroll savings of some sort.
If there is a hardship as a result of this clause it can only be on the employee. He is the one who pays the shot, and he is the one who is asking for it. All it does in effect is to give the unions the merest and barest measure of union security, and the purpose of it is to maintain the strength and integrity of the union.
I am sure the committee will agree with me that a responsible employer should welcome a responsible union. As a matter of fact, in a great number of collective agreements they have the check-off. But there are some who refuse to give it to their employees, for some reason or other, and those who deny it do so,
I think, with the view that they will keep the union weak, because the inability of the union to obtain enough money in order to carry out administration leads to a weak and struggling union. I think the committee will agree with me that it increases the number and the bitterness of conflicts arising in labour-management relations.
We have seen in the past that unions do not starve very easily. They are used to austerity; consequently it never succeeds. Nevertheless the refusal of the employer to be a help to the union leads to difficulties. I call the attention of the committee to a statement made by Mr. Justice Rand in the famous Ford motor case:
I consider it entirely equitable that all employees should be required to shoulder their [The Deputy Chairman.]
portion of the burden of expense for adininister-mg the lan of their employment, the union contract, that they must take the burden along with the benefits.
I am not suggesting that we go that far, although Mr. Justice Rand's decision was hailed as a most progressive one, and it has brought us peace in the automobile industry.
This resolution does not suggest that we go that far. It does not suggest that anyone who is not a member of the trade union should contribute. What it says in effect is that when those who are members make the request of the employer, the employer shall comply with it. I think the request is a simple one. Labour lias not only earned it but deserves it. For a long time they have asked for union security. I think labour relations in this country will improve as we meet labour at least half way.

I said a great deal about this matter when it was in committee, and I am frank to admit that there is a fundamental difference of opinion as to what a collective bargaining agreement is and what it is not. As I said in the committee, I take the British view. I am frank about that. I was raised in the school in which the union officers collected the dues. They had the contact between the officers or the stewards and the men. I think that is the proper way. I do not believe that a provision which comes within the purview of collective bargaining should be written into an act of parliament. I think that approach is fundamental.
I intend to take the long view. I know that at the moment a great deal of confusion exists in the world. It is seen in France, in the United States, in Great Britain, and to a much larger extent in Australia and in other countries. I do not think there is any substitution for people sitting around the table and negotiating an agreement. It has been stated that the check-off exists in some industries in this country. I have no objection to the checkoff as such. I have no objection to a trade union agreement fashioned and negotiated by men sitting around a table. But as I pointed out early in the committee proceeedings, this biff is intended' to go down the middle of the road. It is based on the principle of conciliation.
We have witnessed what has happened in the United States, and I offer no criticism of what has happened there. It is a free country, under the two party system, where you get the ebb and flow of opinion on national affairs. The Wagner Act was passed in that country. Let me point out to my trade union friends, and more particularly to those who have had experience in these matters, that some in the United States thought the Wagner Act was a swing too far to the left. Then, by the turn of the wheel-I think it was the hon. member for Calgary West who used' that phrase in the committee-they got the Taft-Hartley measure. I well know the position taken by the hon. member for Calgary West.

And he still
takes it.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext:
As he has a perfect right to do. But in the United States you have a change in the complexion of congress and the senate. Today you have the Taft-Hartley
measure which a great many people must, by the very nature of things, feel is sound legislation in that country. I remember discussing that legislation with some of the higher ranking officials of the American Federation of Labor. After the president had vetoed the bill, they thought it wmuld not get the necessary majority-I forget whether it is two-thirds that is required^in the congress and senate. I said this to them. Most men are activated by the opinions of the people back home. I ask the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre if that is not what motivates him. Is it not the fact that you want to continue on, that you want to be a member of congress, or the senate, or of this House of Commons from now on?
Why?

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext:
"Pourquoi pas," as they say in French. I sometimes wonder myself. But hon. members have seen what happened in the United States. Many of the cherished things enjoyed by labour organizations have been outlawed under the provisions of recent legislation. This bill does not interfere one iota with collective bargaining between employers and employees. If they want a closed shop, they can have a closed shop, tinder the Taft-Hartley legislation they cannot have it. In Canada there are industries which have had the closed shop for over fifty years because both employers and employees believed it was in the best interests of the industry. I am speaking now of the construction industry. What I am fearful of is that with the swing of the pendulum you might get a government which would go much farther to the left than this government, or the opposition, or even my good friends of the C.C.F. On the other hand you may get a government which swings much farther to the right, and which will take away from the labour organizations conditions which have existed in this country for a good many years. That is why I say that the soundest approach to this problem is through negotiation. You start off with legislating for the check-off. You legislate in connection with wages and other working conditions. That has happened in other countries, as I said in the committee.
I was in Germany at the time of the revolution when Hitler obtained power. At that time Germany had the most powerful trade union movement in the history of the world. But. it was so interwoven with the state that when Hitler got. his fingers on the strings, neither the trade unions nor the employers were free agents. They were merely servants of the state. I should like to see our people
Industrial Relations

sit down as free men and bargain collectively, predicated on responsibility.
It has been said, and truthfully, that some employers have made it difficult for trade unions; but let me say that it cuts both ways. I am sjreaking as a trade unionist. Some trade unions have made it difficult for decent employers. Let us be fair about it. In our approach to this problem we cannot have one law for the rich and a different one for the poor, dealing with the same subject. If we do we are in for trouble. I think that is what is fundamentally wrong with the legislation in the United States. That is what was fundamentally wrong with the Wagner Act. You see the disputes with the typographical union in Chicago and in many other cities of the United States, where legislation has deprived that responsible organization of conditions that it has enjoyed for years, and of some conditions which they have enjoyed for a century in some centres in that country. Therefore I say, Mr. Chairman, I would rather see in our federal jurisdiction the railroad labour organizations sit down with the companies and fashion an instrument predicated on this bill, if you like, having due regard for the difficulties of that widespread organization.
The hon. member for Cape Breton South comes from a tightly-knit organization, the miners' organization, where conditions are comparatively easy. There are not many companies; they all live in the same locality.
I am frank to admit that I do not know too much about the details of the railroad industry in this country. I know it in a broad and general way. Speaking from memory, I think there are twenty-eight different organizations involved. All these different organizations collect dues in many localities. Do not forget that they have enjoyed relations with these companies down through the years not excelled by any other labour organization in this country. What has it been due to? It has been because of the ability to see the other fellow's point of view. I think that is a sound approach.
This afternoon one hon. member referred to the Rand formula. How did the Rand formula come about? It came about through the appointment of Mr. Justice Rand as a commissioner. I played some part in the final conclusions of that dispute. In essence it was straight collective bargaining. Mr. Justice Rand's findings were not compulsory, but they were agreed to by both parties to the dispute. That is the proper approach. I am offering no criticism of the Rand formula, but I question very much, outside of the check-off provisions in that formula, whether many trade unions of this country wish to go the

full length of the implications and applications of that formula, taking the long point of view.
I do not think there is much more I need to say. I like to see meetings such as we have in my organization where everybody turns up and pays his dues. We had good meetings. If they did not turn up to pay their dues the stewards collected them. I know some of the implications when that does not have to be done. I agree with the hon. member for Spadina that i't makes it easy for the trade union organization, but taking the long view-and I say this sincerely on the basis of principle itself-I think it is in the best interests of the trade unions themselves, and I think my prediction will be borne out in the light of experience, that they do the work themselves and not let somebody else do it for them.

I am glad to see that we have a fairly well filled house. It is unfortunate to have this discussion take place at this time. The industrial relations committee gave a lot of thought, and had a lot of discussion on this particular subject. The minister used the same arguments in the committee that he is using in the house today. Nevertheless, by a majority vote of the committee the provision for a check-off was written into the bill. It surprised me this afternoon to have a private member on the government benches move for the deletion of a clause in the bill which was put there after a lot of consideration. Had it come from the minister I would have thought it was the government's intention to have it removed, but since a private member moved it, I am assuming 'that every member on that side of the house will be able to cast his vote freely without being influenced by the cabinet statement made by the minister.
We always do.

Perhaps that will happen. I hope that the assumption of the hon. member for Spadina and of myself is correct, namely, that it merely comes from one private member who perhaps is not as well informed on the subject as he should be.
We are attempting to lay down a national labour code. The objective of that code is to bring uniformity in labour relations between province and province. It is a start, and a good one. But if we remove the clause that we are now discussing, it will make it impossible for provinces such as Manitoba, Saskatchewan, British Columbia, New Brunswick and Nova Scotia to come within the scope of this national code, if the government

Industrial Relations
wish to hand jurisdiction in labour relations over to the provinces; because each of the provinces that I have mentioned has a trade union act, and the check-off provision is written into every one of those acts. In many cases it was not written into those acts with the good will of the employers. It was fought for. The general public of the provinces that I have mentioned are convinced that the principle which we are attempting to lay down in this national code is a good one. I do not think that the governments in the provinces-I am reasonably sure of Nova Scotia- or the general public would want this provision removed. We are defeating the purpose of a national code if we make it impossible for the provinces I have mentioned to come in.
The minister made the statement that in his own union the shop steward collects the dues. That is understandable. Where you have a plant with a small craft union, and the shop steward has forty or fifty men in the shop with him, it is a simple matter to pick up the dues from them. It is not so simple in mass industries. In the gold and nickel mines, the coal mines, and the steel plants, where the unions are organized on an industrial basis, and where you have perhaps four, five or six men administering the affairs of the union, it is impossible to collect dues in that way.
I know that, because we tried it. For years we had the check-off in our agreement in Nova Scotia with the mine workers. In 1932 we thought, we would try collecting dues, and we discontinued the check-off by referendum of our membership. We tried that for two years. It is absolutely impossible for union officials in a mass industry to administer the affairs of the organization by picking up the dues individually. It just cannot be done. By a referendum vote we restored the check-off.
In the organization of the steelworkers for example, I know that for years the steelworkers in Sydney tried to form a collective bargaining organization. This was before the provision for collecting dues was written into the trade union act of Nova Scotia. It never succeeded until that provision was written in. Then the membership put their cards in, and their dues were collected.
What we have to remember is what the hon. member for Spadina has pointed out. There is nothing compulsory about this. You put a card in, and you can withdraw it any time you see fit. The principle is well established. The government itself collects income tax in that way. Church dues are collected in that way.

The minister and the rest of the members of the House of Commons will have to come to a realization of the fact that the trade union movement in this country is a permanent institution. Whether you like it or not, it is here to stay. You will have to remember that the unions have gone through the fighting stage; that day is over. The matter has now entered the administrative stage. Today the unions have as well trained personnel in their leadership nationally, provincially and locally as we have in many departments of government. The signing of a collective agreement is a simple matter today when the unions are organized. The mechanics of it are worked out. I think the days of strikes are practically over, if decent and sensible mechanics are worked out and some rule of law applied to the union movement. If they are given recognition as business people, rather than having to go out on the streets to fight things out, that stage is over. It is relatively simple to sign a collective agreement today.
After the agreement is signed, the union then is not just sitting on the side; it is a community affair. A union which has a responsibility in any community is the biggest asset that community can have. When their dues are coming in, and they can budget on their income, they can take their men forward by way of educational programs, the promotion of co-operative credit unions, playgrounds, and all that kind of thing.

I suggest that hon. members give this matter serious consideration, and that they vote quite freely. The amendment has been moved by a private member. I feel strongly on the point, because I realize the value of the proposal. I see in this democracy in action. It is a recognition of the fact that a man who has a right to put a card in or take it out has a responsibility. There is no section of Canada today in which the check-off provision is operative under the trade union legislation where the unions are not 100 per cent organized. Not a man is out of them; they come in voluntarily, and they are glad to do it that way. In the final analysis they spend that money themselves, through their meetings and by their vote. They receive regular financial reports showing how every dollar is paid out and what came in. It enables the executive of the union which is a rather small body to do a decent job of administration and carry on considerable community work which is not possible under the other system where you must travel from door to door to pick up your dues.
The minister referred to the shop, stewards in craft- organizations and the method of collecting dues as advocated by the bill. There is no comparison. In most large industries you just could not have enough men to do it in that way.

When this matter was being discussed in the committee I asked the hon. member for Spadina if it was to be compulsory or voluntary, and I was informed that it was to be voluntary. I cannot see that that is so, according to this bill.

I am an employer of some consequence; I have not had a union in my organization, and I have employed hundreds of men and women. There has been complete harmony in our relations. We pay over the union rates; we have cafeterias and recreation rooms, and. as I say, there is complete harmony between employer and employee. In the majority of factories on the North American continent that same harmony exists. This is not due entirely to the terrific activities of the unions on behalf of their brothers; it is due to the fact that the employer is just as human a man as any member of any union. He is keenly desirous of bettering the welfare of his workers, providing better working conditions and proper scales of pay adequate to meet the increased cost of living. That is the thought of most employers on the North American continent today.
Much of the discord that exists at the present time is not the result of discontent between employer and employee. The seamen's unions is an example. In that case the strike is not because of differences between employer and employee. The throwing of bricks, the bashing of heads and the utter disregard of the law of this country is due to discontent between union members. It is not all bread and butter garnished with cheese so far as union members are concerned.
I am in favour of holidays with pay; I am in favour of minimum wages; I am in favour of better working conditions and old age pensions for everybody; I am in favour of giving the people of this country anything that they can afford. But I am not in favour of promising them things that I know the}7 cannot afford. They have to pay the piper. The labour people pay the shot.
I know of unions today that have taken union dues without consulting their members and have given them to a political party. One union called a meeting supposed to be for purely business purposes. The by-laws of this union state clearly that no political questions shall be discussed at meetings. But the bylaws were ignored and they went on to discuss the C.C.F. party and all that they would promise. They attempted to discredit the two old parties. This went on until several members of the union rose and reminded the advocates of the C.C.F. party and their principles that they could not discuss the matter
further, that they were using the dues of the union for the purpose of sponsoring the C.C.F. party throughout Canada. We should not attempt to enact a law which would force a man to abide by the decision of radical advocates of certain political parties in this country. Every man should have the right to say, "I will contribute to this if I so wish." The government of Canada has no right at any time to say, "This is what you must do or pay a fine."
On a point of order
The hon. member will have plenty of time when I am through.

There is no other way to deal with this matter than to bring out the true facts to show that this amendment should be supported.
Another reason for supporting the amendment is that they are asking for legislation that will take away the liberties of the working men just as has been done in Russia. As has been mentioned by the minister, there are no trade unions in Russia. Hitler took away the rights of the trade unionists. Certain unions in Collingwood tried to take away the rights of the workers. That was not done by the employers; it was done by the trade unions. Many of these men do not want to contribute to any party. They have the right in this dominion, which I hope they will never lose, of supporting any party which will bring in good and honest legislation for both employer and employee.
I am not seeking the votes or support of any class of person in this country. I am seeking the respect of labour and employers for speaking truthfully and without fear. I hope I shall never deviate from that course. I am strongly against the check-off system because of the abuses by certain unions.

All churches collect their fees in that way. The amount I give is entirely up to me, but the check-off is the method by which it is collected.

During the war years the check-off was one of the most important issues in collective bargaining, and it became a part of the agreements which most large industrial firms made with their employees. That is true, and personally I would much prefer to have every trade union member pay his dues voluntarily as a part of his duty to his union. Let me read the first four lines of the proposed subclause 3 to show that there is nothing compulsory about it:
Upon request of a trade union entitled to bargain collectively under this act on behalf of a unit of employees and upon receipt of a request in writing signed by any employee in such unit, the employer of sueli employee shall, until the employee in writing withdraws such request, periodically deduct and pay out of the wages due to such employee, to the person designated by the trade union to receive the same, the union dues of such employee. . . .
Could anything be freer than that? If we are to assume that the employee has a duty to his union, he surely could not do less than that. I have the highest regard for the experience and wisdom of our Minister of Labour, but in this particular instance I am afraid I find myself in agreement with the hon. member for Cape Breton South and the hon. member for Vancouver East.
Twenty years ago I was timekeeper in a logging camp and I did that in the evenings after I got through work. I found it most desirable, instead of having to procure cash and hand it to the boys for the payment of union dues, to have them give me their names, and at the end of the month I paid the money over to the proper official who forwarded it to the union. It was a voluntary check-off.
Many of the large employers in British Columbia resisted it vigorously at that time, but it never seemed to me that there was anything wrong with that system and I regarded it as both efficient and fair. I could never bring myself to feel that if anyone asked me courteously, as in fact they always did, to take that- money off his pay and hand it to another person, there was anything wrong in my doing so merely because I did it in respect of union dues. I did not consider it any more wrong than if it were done with regard to the Red Cross, or tobacco or chocolate bars or anything else of value.
I, too, am an employer of labour in a small way, and I should not like to have the committee of the whole turn down the amendment that has been proposed by the industrial relations committee, because I feel that the Canadian people would regard this House of Commons as being ten or twenty years behind

the thinking of the provincial legislatures, certainly the thinking of our more progressive legislatures, though judging from some of the acts that have been passed by some of the legislatures one would not suppose that they were far advanced in their thinking.
I am in agreement with the amendment proposed by the industrial relations committee and opposd to the amendment moved by the hon. member for Timiskaming.

I have spoken at least twice in this House of Commons in times gone by in favour of the voluntary revocable check-off and I have not changed my mind. I will therefore oppose the motion proposed by the hon. member for Timiskaming, and may I add that I will do so in spite of the speeches made in opposition to that motion by the members for Cape Breton South and Vancouver Bast.
I do not think it does our cause any good to start political bickering on a subject of this kind, which is quite serious to a great many people. I approach this question in a somewhat different way from that which has hitherto been adopted by persons who have spoken on it, with the exception perhaps of what was said by the last speaker, the hon. member for Comox-Alberni.
In conversation with different people, I have found that the word "compulsory" has been used by many with reference to this matter. There is nothing compulsory about it. A man voluntarily signs an assignment to give some of his own money to someone else; and at any time, in writing, in the same way as that in which he made the assignment, he may then withdraw that assignment and collect his own money. If there is anything in that which is compulsory I at least am utterly unable to find it.
I know it will be said by some people, who perhaps have no great understanding of labour, that advantage will be taken of this, and that certain persons will back a chap up against the wall and say, "Sign on the dotted line." It may be that there are odd instances of that kind in industrial relations. If there are, I believe it is because of the quick growth of unions, certainly since the beginning of the last war, and any great movement of the kind will produce some irresponsible leaders. The actions of such irresponsible people find their way into the headlines of the newspapers, but I prefer to regard these union organizations as being in the main composed of sensible people, just as sensible as we are on a broad plane in this house.
Let us suppose that I am working for someone. I have an employer and I owe a bill to 
a druggist or a grocer or someone else. I give my grocer or my druggist an order on my employer to pay that bill. He will not refuse to do it; he dare not refuse, because it is enforceable at law as an assignment of money. The same thing is true today with respect to wages, even though the assignment goes to a union secretary.
My position, therefore, is simply this. All that this amendment does, as moved in the committee, is to affirm a right which the workman has always had at law to assign his money to whomsoever he wishes, be it his wife, a grocer or a union.
h e have to go back in our consideration of this matter. Everyone in this house has said he believes in collective bargaining. If we believe in collective bargaining we must mean something when we say that, and collective bargaining is bargaining by people without the cards being all in the hands of a man on one side of the table. It is a complete negation of the words "collective bargaining" if it be between one chap who has all the cards and a gun on his hip, and the fellow across the table who has only a couple of white chips. To give it meaning, it must mean that people have the right to meet together and negotiate on something like an even basis.
It has been said that expense is involved. I believe there is some small expense. I have no doubt that the unions would be quite prepared to meet that little expenditure for an extra bookkeeper or whatever it might mean. But I put this to the committee in the way I have done because I have thought this matter over for years. It is not a recent conversion with me. I have spoken about it in the house ever since I came here in 1945. I have spoken about it all across the country, and I have yet to hear from any person a single argument that I could regard as satisfactory, aside from the small question of expense
That is so with one exception; and that has come to my notice only within the past few days. We have jurisdiction here over railways because they are interprovincial. I have learned that those railways going from one ocean to the other are dealing with twenty-eight different unions. It may be that in that case difficulties will arise because of differences in the amount of dues collected by the various unions. That may mean considerable difficulty and perhaps some expense in connection with those brotherhoods. But it must be remembered that the railway people have not this system, nor have they asked for it. They are a set of unions that have carried on up to this time without feeling that there was any necessity for anything of the kind. But to come back to what was said before, they

are craft unions; they are in smaller groups and are spread clear across the country.
So I close, Mr. Chairman, by making this simple statement. I will vote against the amendment as proposed, but not for the reason, as suggested by the hon. member for Cape Breton South and the hon. member for Vancouver East, that there is any political kudos to be obtained from it. I desire to express my opinion with regard to this question. I am greatly surprised this afternoon to find out that the minister is now objecting to the amendment which carried in the committee. This question was thoroughly gone into in the committee, and it passed there by a majority vote. Surely the opinion of that committee, which was given the duty of examining most carefully this bill in all its aspects, should be given a little consideration at this time.
I have had a little bit of experience with this union check-off business myself, because when I was teaching in Alberta we had a union known as the Alberta teachers' association. In that union there was a check-off. Those of us who paid dues into the union were obliged to fight all the battles. Then those who did not participate by paying their dues, shared in the profits. I can say that the picture has now been changed in Alberta and we have the check-off there. In fact, in their forward labour legislation, I think Alberta leads all the other provinces in Canada. This is not something new. It was thoroughly discussed in the committee. It was passed there by a majority vote, and for the life of me I do not see why it should be brought up again. It is something that is not compulsory. It is voluntary in every sense of the word, as was pointed out by the hon. member who preceded me. I do not intend to cover the arguments which he and other hon. members have used. I wish to say I am firmly of the opinion that the voluntary check-off is the proper method of procedure. I shall support it, and I shall vote against the amendment which is now before the committee.

I should like to ask one question. I was not a member of the committee on industrial relations. I have listened to the discussion this afternoon, and I am not clear about this matter. According to those who support the amendment it makes no difference. If it makes no difference, I should
like to know the purpose of it. Am I to understand that the members of the union who wish to pay their dues-and I suppose they all do-are so irresponsible that they cannot be trusted to do so but must have them deducted at the source? This provision seems strange to'me. As I say, if there is no purpose in it, and if there is no reason behind it, why should it be introduced? Would the mover please explain that to me before I vote?

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: The amendment made by the committee to section 32 struck out subsection 8.

I intend to move an amendment to re-insert subsection 8. The subsection originally read as follows:
In any proceedings before the conciliation board, no person except with the consent of the parties shall 'be entitled to be represented by a barrister, solicitor or advocate and, notwithstanding such consent, a conciliation board may refuse to allow a barrister, solicitor or advocate to represent a party in any such proceedings.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Moved by the hon. member for Vancouver East that section 32 be amended by re-inserting subsection 8.

Before you put the amendment, Mr. Chairman, I wish to say a few words in explanation. This subsection has been in the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act since it was first passed in 1907. So far as I know, there was never any strong objection raised to it, nor do I think it has ever interfered with conciliation proceedings. Labour organizations are afraid that if lawyers are allowed to take part in conciliation proceedings it will prove detrimental to the smooth operation of such proceedings.
The minister will remember that the Trades and Labour Congress of Canada gave this bill their endorsation this year and also to Bill No. 338 last year; but he will also remember that a few days ago the executive withdrew the endorsation of the congress from the bill, largely because of the two amendments made to it in committee. One of the amendments made in committee had to do with section 2, subsection (1), paragraph (i), subparagraph (ii). This morning the minister remedied the objection to that section by restoring to the bill what it contained when it was first introduced in the house. Perhaps a stronger objection of the trades and labour congress is taken
 -
to the removal of subsection 8 of section 32. I suggest to the minister that he would be improving the bill by putting it back where it was for the last forty years. It gave good satisfaction to all concerned.
I do not wish to create any controversy in regard to this matter, but it should be remembered that representatives of labour and representatives of the Canadian Bar Association have opposite reasons for having this subsection in or out of the bill, as the case may be. Labour representatives are anxious to have conciliation boards finish their work as quickly as possible, because they begin to receive the benefits when the conciliation proceedings are finished and an agreement is drafted. If lawyers are permitted to take part in the proceedings they will receive the benefits as long as the conciliation board is sitting, and the longer it takes to reach an agreement, the more they will get out of it. I can understand why they would want this section deleted. But let us remember that we are now considering a bill to make conciliation of labour disputes as smooth as possible. We are not drafting a bill to give employment to somebody, no matter to what organization he may belong. I suggest to the minister that it would be a good gesture on his part to take the position that he took when this bill was drafted and support the restoration of this subsection to section 32.

I think I am far enough away from the legal profession to be able to speak with a certain amount of detachment on this issue. I should think all my legal earnings, if added together, would not support a family of five at the present cost of living for more than about two weeks.
I should like to make a few comments on this. In the first place, I find the speeches of the hon. member for Vancouver East so satisfactory that I wish he would not descend to what- he did this afternoon when he suggested that members of the legal profession would regard a conciliation board as a means of spinning out the thing as long as they could in order to make fees. There are lawyers like that, no doubt, but I do not think there are many. I would doubt whether any intelligent organization would be hiring a lawyer like that, because the kind of lawyers who are worthwhile do not have to spin things out. They usually have more jobs than they can perform.
The second thing I wish to say-and here I might seem to be inclining to the views of the hon. member for Vancouver East-is that it is quite often wise not to have lawyers. There are cases where people have a sort of superstitious feeling about retaining lawyers,

Industrial Relations
because of the superstition that they may be able to work magic. They do not work magic at all.
There may be many cases where they should not go in; but it seems to me foolish to suggest that we should have a law or continue a law to keep them out. Why should we keep anyone out who, it is considered by any of the parties to a proceeding, can help? It seems to me just like refusing to let the light in. It seems to me a counsel of darkness, and to my mind it is one of the most retrograde things one might have to consider. Surely we should be ready to let anybody in who has a contribution to make. And if an intelligent union or an intelligent employer wishes to employ a lawyer, why should it or he not do so?
The next point is that there may have been a time, when it would have been suggested- although I observed that the hon. member for Vancouver East did not suggest it-that if lawyers were allowed to come in, the odds would all be tilted against the union. I doubt if anyone will suggest, after the discussion we have heard this afternoon, that in these days unions are poor and down-trodden and cannot get the best lawyers available.
My final point is that it seems to me that to suggest that the presence of lawyers would have the effect of spinning out an investigation and unnecessarily delaying it is to suggest that the chairman is a fool. I do not believe conciliation boards are presided over by fools. They are usually intelligent people. I was one once myself, for a few moments, but I got through very quickly-although I must add that there were no counsel present.
I suggest seriously, however, that to offer the argument that, in order to have proper expedition in carrying out these matters no counsel should be present, is a very poor compliment indeed to those who preside over these boards. I should feel very regretful if we had to continue to countenance a piece of legislation of this kind.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext:
Perhaps lawyers could take care of this thing themselves; but I am in charge of piloting this bill through the House of Commons. The Minister of Labour is fair game for everybody, both in and out of the house. I do not know what some people would do if they had not an opportunity to criticize the secretary of labour in the United States, or if they could not take a pot-shot at the Minister of Labour in Canada, particularly when they lack responsibility and courage themselves-and I do not reflect upon anyone in the committee when I say that.
I must say, however, that, speaking frankly,
I believe this is class legislation. That is my view in the matter. lit was put in there because it was in the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act. It was asked for by the Trades and Labour Congress of Canada and by other labour organizations. But it was put in the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act a good many years ago.
I have had some experience in labour negotiations in my day, and I know the hon. member for Vancouver East has had expert ence, too. I do not know of anyone I would rather be up against than a lawyer. I speak with no disrespect for lawyers, but first of all you have to teach them what you know, yourself. I would rather express my own opinions in my own simple way on the issues in dispute.
And do not forget this, that a disbarred lawyer can get in.
Mr. MaeINNIS: He is not a lawyer, though.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext:
I know of a disbarred
lawyer-
But he has legal training.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext:
I know of a case not long ago for which I was severely criticized, in which a disbarred lawyer's argument was used against me, and against others both in and out of the house. He can plead before one of these boards, and can represent anyone. I know of a member of the house-he happens to be on this side-who is a member of a labour organization and who has served his organization with credit and distinction.
I believe I said on another occasion that you cannot pass a law to turn a sinner into a righteous man. Neither can you pass a law to make sure that someone will not hire the best possible advice. Let us consider the men in the labour movement at the present time. I know of a recent board hearing in the city of Montreal -which was handled by a man who grew up in the labour movement. I am convinced that, although these people speak in simple terms, they possibly know the intricacies of an industry better than any other people.
Then let us consider the industry with twenty or thirty employees. Someone asks for an agreement. What does the manager do? He flies to his lawyer, because he does not know how to develop the case himself. I hope I shall live to see the day in Canada when, even outside the legal profession, there will be those who will specialize in this kind of work. I do not think it is a forbidden field, or a field into which a man in civilian life, irrespective of his calling, could not make his
Industrial Relations

contribution toward what might be described as normal labour conditions in the country.
I have said there is a powerful argument which can be made on the suggestion that this is class legislation which, in effect, denies the right of a livelihood to a certain group of persons in Canada. We have been discussing freedom, and all that kind of thing-what the hon. member for Lake Centre talks about-
Human rights.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext:
God bless human rights, yes. We have been discussing that. Then in the same breath we deny the right to a group of people to earn a livelihood. That is my approach to the matter. I believe it is the commonsense approach and, in the light of conditions as they exist today, I think it is a good one.
What is happening in the United States in this connection? I do not know whether I saw the picture or whether someone told me about it, but the other day John L. Lewis was walking with seven good lawyers along with him.
Was it Lewis?

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext: Yes, absolutely. What does one always do? What do we do-entirely outside labour disputes-when we get into trouble, whether it be civil or some other kind of trouble? We go to a lawyer. Of course we do.
It is not a compulsory measure.

For many years past I have lad connection with labour organizations and .r.dustrial strikes in the police department, fire and street departments, the post office, and the street railway departments. It has been my experience that, while lawyers have their usefulness in certain kinds of activities, they are absolutely useless in most industrial disputes.
I have had a wide experience in labour activities. While I am a lawyer myself, I believe those disputes might well be left to the parties, so that they might choose conciliators from among themselves and settle matters. I believe the section was all right as it was drafted. A board of conciliation should be able to settle a dispute as between man and man.
Let us consider the workmen's compensation act. I can remember when the present minister was a controller in the city of Hamilton. The matter came up as to whether they would allow lawyers before that workmen's compensation board which was dealing with the case of an

employee who had beien injured. It was decided' by the Ontario legislature that it would not be in the interests of either the employer or the employee in the case of an accident in industry to allow lawyers to plead before the board when a settlement could be brought about without their doing so.
I understand that, according to the labour law, both federal and provincial, the minister or the deputy minister of labour can intervene and try to bring the parties together. That is the whole principle of the industrial disputes act. I was a member of the committee on industrial relations for nineteen years-I am not a member now-and my experience is that, while lawyers have their place, it is not here. In saying this, I am not against anybody or any business or profession.

I am surprised at the attitude taken by some hon. members against the legal profession. We are led to believe that if lawyers are permitted to appear before conciliation boards the proceedings will be protracted for their personal benefit, but I have not heard one good reason why the legal profession should be singled out. This discussion has been going on for fifteen minutes and nothing has been achieved; yet not one lawyer member has taken part in it. I think that is a clear example of the possibility of obtaining a quick decision in these matters.
I do not think any one profession should be singled out by legislation passed by this house. The parties to a dispute may call in accountants or skilled men from other professions, but the members of the legal profession are barred. Yet the question that may be troubling the conciliation board may be a question of law.
The great majority of lawyers spring from the labouring classes. Thousands of lawyers in this country have worked for years and years for the labouring men without receiving one cent of remuneration. Time and time again I have opened up cases which had been before conciliation boards where the decision had been against workmen when I knew they were right. I have done that in hundreds of cases without receiving one cent of remuneration, and there are thousands like me in this country. It is unfair to single out the legal profession and bar them from appearing before a conciliation board when the parties themselves want such assistance.

I hesitate to say anything about this amendment, because I am not a member of the committee on industrial relations. I understand that, as the bill was originally brought in, it contained this sub-

Industrial Relations
section 8 which bars lawyers from appearing before a board. Then the committee in its wisdom decided that the subsection should be removed, the effect being that lawyers would be permitted to appear.
I do not think the hon. member for Vancouver East spoke with his usual fervour and conviction when he moved his amendment today. As he spoke, I thought of the many times when he has spoken in this house on the rights of the downtrodden and of minorities, all worthy subjects, but today I am afraid his tongue was in his cheek.

Mr. Chairman, I object to the hon. member for Vancouver South attributing any insincerity to me in connection with this matter. I debated the matter in committee in the same way as I have debated it today. If the hon. member is accustomed to speaking with his tongue in his cheek, I am not.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I think the hon. member should withdraw that remark.

That was the point I was making, that the hon. member does not usually speak with his tongue in his cheek. If the hon. member objects, I am quite happy to withdraw the remark. This is a most serious matter for the members of the legal profession. I am a member of that profession and I have no regrets over belonging to it. It is a great profession which has contributed a great deal, not- only to the public life of Canada but to the welfare of those who have the hardest time. There is no reason why that profession should be singled out in this bill. I have a resolution here which was passed by the Vancouver bar association, one recital of which sums up the picture from the point of view of the legal men. It reads:
And whereas such provision is the negation of the democratic rights of parties before conciliation boards and is an unwarranted restriction imposed on and discrimination against a section of the public in the conduct of a profession which has contributed much to the public life and welfare of Canada . . .
I think that sets forth the situation. About ten j^ears ago I had the privilege of acting as chairman of an arbitration board considering a dispute between the new'spaper proprietors in Vancouver and the typographical union. The case for the union was presented by a representative who was brought in from San Francisco and whose business it was to appear before arbitration boards. He was not a larvyer. but he was a skilful labour representative. I do not think any lawyer in Canada could have made a better presentation than that representative from San Francisco. No
5849-342J
one had any quarrel with his being brought from San Francisco to present the case. It does seem to me that there is no reason why a Canadian lawyer should not be allowed to appear, either for the union or for the other side. I urge hon. members of the committee who are not of the legal profession to report the bill as it was reported from the committee.

I do not think the hon. member for Vancouver South and others who have argued that lawyers are being debarred from conciliation boards are reading the section correctly. There is nothing in the subsection which the hon. member for Vancouver East wants restored that would debar lawyers from attending hearings if they are requested! so to do, or if the board chairman feels that they are necessary. There is nothing in the subsection that would indicate any particular1 discrimination against that profession. If the hon. member will read the subsection he wilt see that that is the case.
By this legislation we are setting up labour jurisprudence for the handling of labour disputes, wage disputes and so on. This is not criminal law; this is not the type of statute which the legal profession is trained to handle. When we were refusing the right to engineers to bargain collectively I did not hear one word from hon. members who have taken part in this discussion. Apparently there were no human rights involved there. I did not hear them speak when we were refusing the right of check-off on a voluntary basis.
We must recognize the fact that for the first time we are setting up a national rule of law to govern labour relations. Under the section as it was in the original bill and which we are seeking to have restored, authority is placed in the hands of the board and the parties to the dispute to call counsel if they so desire. I do not think the argument that was used by the very capable member of the legal profession who has just taken his seat was valid, as I think he will agree if he reads the clause we wish restored.
While on this matter of lawyers, among whom I have some great friends, I have a clipping in my hand from a United States publication called Labor, which the Minister of Labour probably knows, and this is what it has to say in an editorial on the railway dispute in the United States. The editorial is headed "Lawyers", in big letters and says:
"Almost from beginning to end, one of the real troubles in this dispute has been that railroads have shifted their responsibilities over to lawyers," a union leader declared. "For example, during the emergency board hearings, they had a battery of 16 lawyers to handle their case, while we had only one.
Industrial Relations

"Thus, collective bargaining on the 'Iron Horse' has degenerated into litigation. You can't have peace on the rails that way."
He is complaining that you do not have enough lawyers.
No, he is not. He is complaining that the railroad companies, with unlimited funds, can hire a battery of high-priced lawyers to fight a struggling union which can afford to hire only one.
They are going to spend a million to defeat the president, so they must have money.

It was sixteen lawyers to one :in that case. But the point I want to make is that there is no suggestion in the clause that lawyers should be kept out. It is merely placing the matter in the hands of the judge and the parties to the dispute, and, in the final analysis, in the judgment of the chairman of the board. The minister says he has a wonderful board. I do not see, then, why he should mistrust them. This provision has been in the act for a long time, and if labour is going to accept its responsibilities it should begin to handle its own problems.
I have no doubt that the unions in Canada today have in their own organizations personnel qualified to handle any labour problem that would come within the scope of this act. My experience with negotiations has been this. If we needed a lawyer we went out and got one, and the best time and place to see him was before the negotiations began, having him sit down in an office and prepare a memorandum which would help to get the facts straightened out in our own minds before we went into the negotiations-not after we went in. No one is able to handle negotiations dealing with wages and economic conditions better than the people who are actually involved in the dispute and know the basic facts. If legal advice is required the best time to take it is before the negotiations begin, when you are preparing your brief for submission to the board. I hope that the hon. member for Vancouver South will take another look at this clause, and if he does I am sure he will find that it gives ample scope for the legal profession to appear if,-in the judgment of the board, that is necessary.

This is coming pretty close to home, since up to now I have got my living by the practice of law. Of course I do not need to do that any more, now that I am getting so well paid for being in Ottawa six months of the year.
It seems to me that perhaps we are overlooking the most important thing in this whole discussion which has centred around large cor-

porations and large labour unions:	But that
does not present a true picture of the industrial situation in Canada at all. Where I live we have only one large industrial organization, engaged in the mining of coal. We had another fast-growing organization, which is not as yet unionized, searching for oil. On the other hand, we have many small industries employing, say from fifteen to twenty men, and in Ontario and Quebec there are many organizations of that kind.
The ordinary labour union is, as a rule, a member of one of the two or three major national labour organizations in this country. In the event of a dispute and conciliation proceedings before a board the union has immediate access to the best advocates that I know of in the labour business, and they are contained within the labour organization itself. They are excellent advocates because they have had much experience in this work. But the employer who must meet the union in conciliation proceedings is a man who, as a rule, has risen from his bench and perhaps got his own shop and has made it grow. He is not equipped to present his own case to the tribunal. He has had no experience in public speaking, and' has no conception of putting together things on a paper called a brief in a manner that will be readable, so that he is unable to present his case in the best light. For that reason, if for no other, he should be able to employ a lawyer .to assist him.
I have heard this story before about lawyers spinning things out and taking a long time. But the employers could easily circumvent the law. All they have to do is to name a lawyer as the third person on the board, which usually consists of three people. But that would not be right; that would not be honest. So the proper thing to do is to have a lawyer who will present your case in the best way possible.
Furthermore, we know that the large labour organizations are well equipped, not only with lawyers but with research people, economists, accountants and all that kind of thing. So the day is long since gone when there is any virtue or anything bona fide in the cry that labour cannot employ lawyers to meet those of the corporations. The hon. member for Cape Breton South gave as an illustration the railway dispute in the United States, where the railroads had sixteen lawyers to one representing the union. But we all know that this union is among the wealthiest in the world. It could buy out, lock, stock and barrel, all the lawyers it could find in any large city in the United States. My view is that anybody who employs sixteen lawyers in the one case is an ass. In my judgment he could not be anything else, because more than half of them

Industrial Relations
would be surplusage and a clog on the wheel in operating any sort of hearing.
One word about the other aspect of it. I am not so greatly concerned about the money that we lawyers make or may not make in connection with this matter, though perhaps some will be. But I am concerned about its being said to us, "You have been trained to examine a new proposition quickly, to find the bones of it, and from those bones to make up a case and present it". Your lawyer of 1918, if he makes money, is not the fellow who is in the courthouse all the time. That was true years ago, but is quite untrue now. There are not in the dominion ten lawyers who are making a living at criminal practice, if we take the big cities and all. Most of the cases now involve persons who have long since lost the ability to pay a lawyer when they get into that kind of trouble.
The lawyer of today is a businessman. His whole training these days is to go into investigations like milk, butter and so on, coal mining and the rest, which are held throughout the country, because he is trained to think in a businesslike way.
As to his spinning things out, I can give my hon. friend one case. I haite to be personal, but this was in connection with the conciliation board in Alberta, and he knew the parties on one side, headed by Bob Livett. It was before the late Mr. Justice MacGillivray. They were at a deadlock; his lordship telephoned me-I happened to know them-and in 'that same afternoon we got a settlement. In that case there was no lawyer except myself who was called by the bench, and I did not prolong the case. I settled it. That is a matter of history, a matter of record.
This story about lawyers going into these things to prolong them, whether the implication is or is not that it is done in order to get money, is the most utter and complete nonsense. I know that organizations had a hard job to get lawyers in the old days in connection with workmen's compensation where every case went before the court. They did not have money. We have been debarred ever since that day from taking our place before certain tribunals, but that went out with the horse and buggy. The unions are stronger financially and in numbers. They are equipped with the very best talent, and I can see no reason why we should not be admitted to serve either them or the employer.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
Is the committee ready for the question? I would point out that what the hon. member for Vancouver East is doing in this amendment is to restore in the bill a clause that was removed in committee.
