speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
Sections 33 to 44 inclusive agreed to.
On section 45-Prosecution of employers' organization or trade union.

There was considerable discussion of this clause in committee and I have a simple amendment to move. I am sure everyone will support it. I move that section 45, subsection 1, be amended by striking out the word "and" in the third line and substituting the word "board" for "organization" and by striking out the words "or union".
Will the hon. member please read the section with the proposed amendment?

The subsection would then
read:
A prosecution for an offence under this act may be brought against an employers' organization or a trade union in the name of the board . . .
The rest of the section would be the same as it is now. My reason for moving this amendment is that in my opinion this section is the meat of the whole act. Unless the board has the responsibility for enforcing the act and the authority to enforce it, I think we are leaving matters of labour relations in Canada pretty much where they are at the present time.
The amendment I now suggest would put-the board in the position where, if it considered either side in an illegal position under the terms of the act, it could institute proceedings in the court against the party committing the infraction. I insist upon this, because we argued it in committee. Unless we place this responsibility and authority in the hands of the board, we are leaving labour relations where they are today, a matter of going through conciliation, a matter of going to the board, or of either employers or unions ignoring boards set up by the government, as has happened in the dispute between the lake shipping companies and the seamen's union.
The government appoints a board. The operators refuse to have anything to do with it. They ignore the law completely, with the result that you have anarchy in that industry today, and the Minister of Labour and the government are the goats. If the board were enforcing the act, as I am advocating now, it would have been in a position to take the offending party to court and have the penalties contained in the act applied.
I do not think there is any court in the country in a better position to determine which side in a dispute is in the wrong than the
Industrial Relations

labour relations board that will administer this act when we get through with it. They sit in and listen to the evidence from both sides. They know who is reasonable and who is unreasonable. In addition to that, if this board has some such authority as we are trying to give to it, both unions and employers will approach it with a more respectful attitude. But if the board is to be merely constituted as a forum, and has no authority whatsoever in the matter of enforcement, these people will do as they have been doing; they just go in and argue the thing; and if they are not satisfied, they walk out. What happens after they are through there? The board has wasted its own time and the money of the government. Then it is a matter of the union's applying to the Minister of Labour for the right to prosecute the employer in the courts, or vice versa. In the seamen's union strike we have a good [DOT]example right at. the present time. This legislation does not work out and cannot work out. Unless we intend to enforce the act, I think we are wasting our time in setting it up.
As I said in a previous debate, I believe that we are now applying the rule of law to labour relations. We are setting up a labour jurisprudence. In my opinion this labour relations board should be a court in which would be determined any infractions of the law and so forth. Then it would be a matter of taking the case to the regular courts to have the penalties imposed. But unless we are prepared to change section 45 in order to give the board that authority to use if it sees fit to do so, we are wasting our time. As I say, I do not think it would be used often. But if both sides knew the board had that power and right, I think they would do everything reasonable and possible to settle their disputes in there before the board, without going out and fighting it out, as they are now doing in the lake shipping strike.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext:
If this amendment
passes, we might as well just wipe out the board and the approach by way of conciliation by the labour department. It is beyond my imagination why people keep on talking and asking why we should not prosecute somebody and why we should not put somebody in jail, when we are dealing with labour disputes; and I would point out that it is not all on either one side or the other, I think the proper view-and it is the one we take- is that if you want a labour court, say so, and establish one.
Let me say this to my hon. friend. The establishment of a labour court is not the answer to the question. It is the easiest thing in the world to make the broad and general statement that if we had a labour court fMr. Gillis.]
everything in the garden would be lovely. Recently there was a disastrous railway strike in the state of Queensland. A labour organization there defied the machinery-we will put it in that way-of the labour court. I have here a copy of the act passed by a labour government in the state of Queensland. People talk about legislation with regard to peaceful picketing and what have you; but I do not know of any piece of legislation in the world that compares with it. Mr. PAUL E. COTE (Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Labour) moved the second reading of Bill No. 343, to amend the Government Annuities Act.
He said: In opening the discussion on the second reading of this bill, I think the house will expect me to give a summary of its amending provisions and the intentions which have governed the recommendations that such changes be implemented. Since its inception in 1908, the Government Annuities Act has not been substantially changed in many ways. The administration of the act was first given to the Department of Trade and Commerce, where it stayed until 1912, when it was transferred to the department of the Postmaster General. In 1922 it was given to the Department of Labour, where it still is. So far as the administrative structure of the act is concerned, there has not been anything done by way of amendment more than to change the minimum or maximum amount of annuity for which a purchaser was permitted to contract. This has been done from time to time.
I believe at this stage I should restrict my remarks as much as possible, and give a sort of perspective of the bill. Net receipts during the thirty-nine years from inception to March 31, 1948, total $462,814,944.90, over 50 per cent of which resulted from operations in the last five years. The rigidity of the present act has become more and more evident with the increasing volume of business. Family responsibilities and the financial status of many annuitants change over the years, and the present act provides little opportunity to alter original contracts to give effect to such changes. The main purpose of the bill is to provide more flexibility by permitting, within limits, the conversion and alteration of annuity contracts.
By reason of the arrangement of section 4 of the act, there is no authority for issuing or changing certain types of annuity contract. This lack of provision in the act defeats to a harmful extent the real objective of the act, namely, to fit each annuitant with the type

Industrial Relations
and, within statutory limits, the kind of annuity best suited to his needs and means and to keep him so fitted during the life of the contract. The proposed amendments to this section extend to purchasers the freedom of choice as to the type and terms of authorized annuity contracts which might be required to meet changing circumstances. Authority to make regulations for the conversion and alteration of annuity contracts which are authorized by the new section is provided under the appropriate section.
The amount of the minimum annuity which may be sold is increased from $10 a year to $60 a year. It has been found that annuities yielding less than $5 a month are of little value to the annuitant and do not warrant the cost or expense involved in the selling, accounting and servicing. The total amount that might be paid by way of annuity or annuities to any annuitant or to joint annuitants has been increased from $1,200 to $1,500.
There is no substantial change involved in the provisions concerning payments in the event of death, but the section has been redrafted for purposes of greater clarity and *certainty. In accordance with the authorized rates, when the holder of an immediate annuity dies no benefit is payable except to the extent of any guaranteed instalments of annuity, and immediate surrender of the purchase money is required. If the annuitant should die before having received even the first instalment of the annuity, the terms of the present act may be invoked to return the purchase money with interest to the heirs. This inconsistency in the benefit presumed in the calculation of rates and the provisions of the present act, has been removed by the amendments to this section. In addition, broader *options are provided to the purchaser as to the disposition of payments under this section in extending the privilege of naming beneficiaries and of commuting guaranteed payments.
The basis to be followed in establishing interest rates is set out and provision made for a review of interest rates and mortality tables at least once every five years and for the return of premium payments in prescribed *circumstances.
The section dealing with the accounts to be kept and the manner in which the liability for annuity contracts in force at the end of each fiscal year shall be calculated, has been redrafted for purposes of greater clarity and certainty. The wording has been discussed with and concurred in by representatives of the office of the auditor general and the comptroller of the treasury.
I submit that for the time being what I have said should be sufficient to open a useful discussion on the principle of the bill. There may be other points which hon. members would wish to clear up and which could be discussed in the house. These latter remarks would be more in order, however, when we reach the committee stage, because they can be related to the different sections of the bill.
I submit that, under these circumstances, the amendments sought to the Government Annuities Act have become necessary. This is the first time in thirty-nine years that an attempt has been made to modernize the administrative structure of the act. In view of the tremendous increase in business which began five or six years ago, it has become necessary to have this matter properly attended to by the house in the manner set out in the bill.
On motion of Mr. Cote (Verdun) the debate was adjourned.

I am glad to see that this bill has read ed the stage of adoption. As you know, Mr Chairman, ever since you

Government Annuities Act
and I came here about nineteen years ago, sixteen years of that time I was a member of the industrial relations committee, and I took part in all the discussions that occurred there during that time. A year or two ago, for reasons unknown to me, I was left off the committee, notwithstanding the fact that I have been a labour man nearly all my life and associated with the operations of labour and big business. Because I did not hear any of the discussions before the committee, I refrainrd from saying anything on the bill, but I should like to say a word or two at this time.
A few moments ago I voted against an amendment which would have reinserted subsection 8 of section 32 in the bill. That subsection had the effect of barring lawyers from appearing before conciliation boards. During my many years in business and my connection with controversies of one kind and another, I know that many lawyers who were honest in their convictions have rendered good service, both to the employees and to the employers. I have in mind several of these gentlemen, but in particular I am thinking of Mr. Bernard Rose, K.C.. of Montreal.
Since there was a possibility that lawyers would be barred from appearing before conciliation boards, I have received many letters of protest. For years it has been the job of Mr. Rose to appear before conciliation boards on behalf of labour, and for that reason I opposed the amendment which would have barred such lawyers from acting in that capacity. Mr. Bernard Rose had the respect of the labour unions and of businessmen. I am glad to see that such lawyers as he is and others like him will now be permitted to appear in the settling of disputes. I am sure the minister knows the man I refer to, and knows many others like him of great ability and honesty of purpose.
I have just a word or two further to say. I was in big business for many years and had much to do with labour and disputes between business and labour. I found that the large majority of labour leaders were honest, upright, devoted men, imbued with the spirit of doing the best they could for the men they represented, but wholly against a strike unless it became absolutely necessary. They have often told me, and it is true, that a strike does not pay either side. It does not pay the working man, because it means he is out of work and without his weekly pay envelope for as long as the strike lasts. It does not pay the employer, because his wheels are not turning and production is stopped. So I am absolutely convinced that the vast majority of labour leaders and of business operators are happy to
avoid a strike and happy to see any dispute between management and labour settled by negotiation. That has been my experience. It is only the odd man in either camp who might want to have a row.
If this bill does what everybody hopes it will do, it will be a very good bill. It is along the lines I have advocated in this house for the past fifteen or sixteen years. There is no reason why the honest labour leader and the honest industrialist cannot sit down together with their feet under the same table and settle their disputes. I have seen it done many times. I have seen only one strike in the line industry in which I was engaged, comprising several plants, for many years, because the labour leaders there were sound, sensible, honest men, who wanted the best they could get for their men, naturally, but wanted, if at all possible, to avoid a strike. That is the type of man, both in labour and in management, that I have been dealing with all my labouring and business life. I have served in the labour ranks and paid my dues in a very large organization with which I was associated many years ago.
I am happy to see this bill pass and trust that it will realize the hopes of all of us.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: PROVISIONS AS TO ISSUE, CONVERSION AND, AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, by an interests ing coincidence, it is exactly forty years ago tomorrow, June 18, 1908, that the Government Annuities Act was given second reading by this House of Commons. When one considers the individualistic ideas of that time, the act was indeed a forward step, and many Canadians have been grateful to the government of Sir Wilfrid Laurier for what they did at that time. I am afraid, however, that Canadians

Government Annuities Act

generally will not feel so grateful about the changes being made in that act by the present government forty years later.
The parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Labour (Mr. Cote), in introducing the bill this afternoon, referred to some of the changes being made as administrative in character. He also said that in some cases the aim is to loosen up the rigidity of the act with respect to altering contracts, and I agree that those provisions are all to the good.
However, there are, in the amending act now before us, at least two provisions which I very much dislike. One of them is the provision that the rate of interest to be used in computing the rates for the purchase of annuities shall be tied to the rate of interest on government bonds, with certain qualifications which I need not go into at this time. That provision confirms the action taken by order in council just before April 19, which resulted in a considerable increase in the cost of annuities as from April 19 of this year. The other change which is provided for in this act and which I deplore is one that actually introduces an element of rigidity which was not there before.
I use that word, because the parliamentary assistant this afternoon boasted of the fact that in some respects the amendment was to get rid of some of the rigidities. I point out to him that this amending bill introduces an element of rigidity not there before, in that, from now on, government annuities will have to be taken out on the understanding that regular payments of the same amount must be made at specified intervals.
Previously it was possible to take out an annuity contract and make payments at any time in almost any amount. I think the minimum acceptable at one time was twenty-five cents. I have no doubt there have been some abuses of the wide latitude which was provided, but it seems to me that the government is going too far toward the other extreme in making contracts so rigid that people will be frightened from taking out government annuities. It will seem to many people another commitment they have to tie themselves to, which they might not be able to meet, and therefore there will be reluctance to take out annuities because of that feature.
I indicated at the outset that this legislation saw its birth in this house forty years ago tomorrow, and the parliamentary assistant has already given figures to indicate its popularity across the years, and in particular, according to the figures he gave this afternoon, its mounting popularity in the last five years or so.
As at March 31, 1948, 210,796 Canadians held annuity contracts. That number is not great

compared with the total population of Canada, but it is a substantial beginning, looking toward the goal which the Minister of National Health and Welfare indicated last night, a contributory old age pension scheme that might enable Canadians to provide adequately for their own old age.
May I remind the house again that the preamble to the original act as passed back in 1908, being chapter 5 of the statutes of Canada for that year, in the reign of Edward VII, read:
Whereas it is in the public interest that habits of thrift be promoted and that the people of Canada be encouraged and aided thereto so that provision may be made for old age; and whereas it is expedient that further facilities be afforded for the attainment of the said objects; therefore His Majesty by and with the advice and consent of the Senate and House of Commons of Canada enacts as follows . . .
Then followed the terms of the act itself. This indicated that even in those days, which are looked upon as having been more individualistic than is the case today, there was recognition of the partnership that could be played by individuals and the community in providing for old age.
On the basis of that legislation, despite the fact that until recently it has been given little advertising or publicity, over 200,000 Canadians now hold contracts. This means that as at March 31, 1948, there were 210,796 Canadians who had the beginnings of a contributory old age pension plan. Of that total figure I have given, 118,733 held what are known as individual contracts, and the rest, 92,063, held certificates in group plans.
May I characterize those two groups of people in another way? What it means is that the 118,733 Canadians who, at March 31 of this year, held individual plans were participants in a two-way contributory old age pension plan. The individuals paid and the government paid a small amount. The others, 92,063, were participants in the really desirable kind of contributory old age pension plan, a three-way plan; the three contributors were the individuals themselves, their employers and the government.
The government's contribution in both cases, until April 19 of this year, consisted of the whole cost of administration of the plan, plus an element of subsidy which came into the picture by virtue of the fact that the rates on annuities were calculated on the basis of a rate of interest a little bit higher than the government would have to pay on the open market. But since April 19, that element of subsidy has in effect been removed; and that new policy is confirmed by the bill now before us. From now on, the rates which must be paid for annuities are based on an interest

Government Annuities Act
i ate which is tied to the going rate of interest on government bonds. In other words, the government is putting into this fund nothing more than what it would have to pay to borrow that money anyway. This means that from now on, when an individual takes out an individual contract, it is a one-way contributory old age pension plan instead of a two-way one. It means that, from now on, individuals who take out certificates in group plans become participants in only a two-way plan, the contributions being paid by the individuals and by their employers, but no longer by the government. It seems to me that this is a step in the wrong direction, and I find it hard to understand the Liberal government of 1948 going back on the good beginning made by the government of Sir Wilfrid Laurier in 1908.
May I remind the house once again that this change in the basic interest rate that is used for computing the cost of annuities has had the effect of increasing the amount that people have to pay in order to buy them? The increases vary according to the type of plan, the age of the purchaser, and other factors; but in the main, if a person is sixty years of age or so, and is putting his savings into an immediate annuity as a lump sum, he will now have to pay about 15 per cent or 16 per cent more than he had to pay prior to April 19. On the other hand, if a person is twenty or twrenty-five years of age or so, and takes out an annuity contract for which he will make periodic payments with a view to the annuity maturing at age sixty or sixty-five, he will have to pay from 36 per cent to 44 per cent more than was the case prior to April 19. That shows up the way in which the element of subsidy has been withdrawn, and it points out the way in which the government's contribution in this contributory scheme has been stopped.
As I have already indicated, it seems to me that is a reversal of a good Liberal policy of 1908, and I am indeed sorry that the government has taken this step. I have expressed this view before on the floor of this house this year, and it was inevitable that a certain amount of correspondence should come to me about this matter. I have been interested in the cross-section of the community from which this correspondence has come. It has come from individuals of small means and from workers, as well as from companies and concerns, who feel that the basis of a good three-way contributory plan has been badly upset.
As I indicated previously, this has the effect of introducing discrimination as between various people. It just does not seem fair that some of us who may have taken out annuity
contracts prior to April 19 are able to buy our old age pension at a cheaper rate than is somebody else of the same age who takes out an annuity contract now. The same thing holds true with regard to employees working for one and the same firm. Employees in a particular firm who held their certificates prior to April 19 are buying their retirement at a cheaper rate than are those who have become members of the same company's group plan subsequently to April 19. I do not like it, and I am sure that the people of Canada feel the same way about it.
A good deal has been said, in defence of the government's action, about the need for keeping the fund actuarially sound. In reply to a question I asked on a former occasion, the Minister of Labour gave figures as to the amount of money that the government was having to put into this fund, not only to pay for the cost of administration but to make up the accruing deficit. The minister said something to the effect that common sense would dictate a change in policy in order to avoid these mounting deficits. I believe the figure-and I will give an outside one-ran to something like $1,500,000 altogether for administration and for making up the deficit for the last year for which the minister gave the figures.
To some people this seems to be a final argument, that we should not be spending money which one might call the meeting of a deficit. Actually it is a subsidy; and, as hon. members know, we in this house certainly subsidize a great many things. Some of us want to see subsidized some things that are not yet on the list-such as food and other necessities the prices of which have gone sky high. But surely this is one thing that is deserving of a subsidy from the public treasury, namely, the attempt of people to help to provide for their owm old age. I know the argument which is sometimes used is that it means that several million people must pay taxes in order to help a few hundred thousand achieve this purpose; but the result is that you make it possible for those few hundred thousand to keep from going on the other old age pension; that, will save money for those who pay taxes. You also get established the beginnings of something that could be enlarged to a universal scheme.
I suggest that the arguments about deficit financing do not hold at all. If we can afford, for example, to forgo $5,000,000 of federal revenue this year in order to make the change in the income tax law that the Minister of' Finance made a few weeks ago, then we can afford $1,000,000, $1,500,000 or $5,000,000 a year for a purpose of this kind, namely, to help

I might say that if you are twenty-five years of age and far-sighted enough to plan ahead to when you will be sixty-five and want to retire on $100 a month, it will cost you $186.12 a year instead of $129.12. or 44 per cent more to do so now with the dominion government annuities than before a recent order in council cut the interest rate from four to three per cent, If you are twenty, the new plan will cost you $151.44 a year instead of $101.28, or an increase of 49-5 per cent; if thirty-five, $295.08 instead of $218.64, or an increase of 35 per cent, and if forty, $385.08 instead of $294.48, or an increase of 30-8 per cent. These figures were listed recently by W. D. Welsford, manager of William M. Mercer Limited, independent pension consultants, to show how cutting the interest rate by one per cent boosted the new rates.
In relation to company retirement plans for their employees, the difference is even more startling. Under the new rates it will cost a

Government Annuities Act
firm 130 per cent more to finance the pension of a forty year old worker than under the old. A firm with five hundred workers, considering a retirement plan based on the annuities, will pay an additional 8150,000 for past employees' service just to get the scheme in operation. In ten years the one per cent interest cut will mean 8200,000 from this one company's treasury.
Setting back mortality tables by three years, in addition to the interest cut, is another blow at the annuities. Such a revision is not justified on the basis of a group plan. Even the insurance companies are not using as stiff a table as this, and they are making money.
Another factor that will affect the popularity of these annuities is that it will no longer be possible to pay odd amounts at odd times at the post office toward the annuity. Hitherto you could pay as little as twenty-five cents a week, or prepay as much as $1,000 if you had the ready cash. Now the annuities are on a firm contract basis, and special arrangements have to be made for prepayment, while arrears must be paid within reasonable limits, according to the government announcement.
However, there is nothing to indicate that people who bought their annuities before April 19 will have to change their method of payment. Keeping the two classes of customers apart may turn out to be an administrative problem of headache proportions. What if the dominion government bonds which now pay 2-05 per cent could not be cashed in at any time? They certainly would not be as popular. Where else can the government borrow money at three per cent, as they will be able to with the new annuities?
Another point is that if the government annuities are made less attractive, it will not mean that pension plans and individual annuities will be purchased from insurance companies instead. It will mean that they just will not be purchased, and the possibility of old age security w'ithin the framework of private enterprise will disappear.
Still another point is that if annuities remain attractive, Canada's expanding population and level of business activity would result in more money being collected by the government in premiums than would be paid out and that this could be an anti-inflationary measure.
Unless cash surrender values are offered, a lowering of the interest rate will mean relatively few government annuities sold. A larger part of corporation funds will be directed to plant investment and the payment of dividends and the important deflationary force will disappear.
An upward movement in interest rates has started which should increase the insurance companies' earnings beyond four per cent. If insurance company contracts did not have to bear such a high loading for commissions and expenses, it should be possible to make them quite competitive with government annuity contracts, particularly since the insurance company contracts offer cash values, and the government annuity contracts do not.
It has been suggested that the 81,200 a year limit should be raised to $2,000, because a couple can no longer retire comfortably on $1,200 a year.
Many people bought annuities by the small payment plan. Parents saved this way to educate their children to fit them for different walks of life. I think our government with the huge surplus on hand have forgotten that perhaps never in the history of Canada have our people found it as hard to make a living and raise and educate their children. It is difficult for most Canadian citizens to understand why the government should lower the interest rate on annuities, while at the same time the policy of the Bank of Canada has been changed so that interest yields on government and other bonds arc increased.
Mr. JOHN R. MacNICOL (Davenport): Mr. Speaker, I am not so sure that the change in the interest rate from four to three per cent will not defeat the purpose the framers of the original act had in mind, namely, to have as many as possible of the lower-paid classes take part in a. government scheme of this kind, because that will increase the cost to the annuitant.

At this particular time it might be wise to call to the attention of the government its niggardly treatment of civil servants. I do not wish to be unkind or unfair, because I think there has been too much said by hon. members opposite about judges' pensions and pensions of transport commissioners; but I do feel that in many departments of government the treatment has not been generous. For instance, I know of a lifeboat man who had worked with the Department of Transport for the last thirty-five years and who had never been given an opportunity by the government to contribute toward his security in old age. The lifeboat man I have in mind retired at the age of sixty-eight with a pension of $40 a month from which the government deducted $17 as back payments, leaving a net pension, after thirty-five years of service, of only $23 a month.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to protest against the action taken on April 19 last by order in council in connection with this matter. I can find no better summary of the effect of the order in council than that which appeared in an editorial in the Ottawa Citizen. It summarizes my viewpoint on the question; indeed I believe it summarizes the viewpoint of many thousands of people throughout the country. I quote from it:
Because of this ill-considered decision sales of annuities to persons of modest means will decrease, the number of employees covered by pension plans will be lessened, the cost of such plans raised unnecessarily and the savings for old age discouraged.
Thi3 annuity plan represented an arrangement between the government of Canada and those who would enter into contracts believing that the provisions of the annuity plan would remain in effect. The changes that were made have never been justified by the minister. At the time of the change he did give an explanation which did not appeal to the reason of many members of this house and of many people in this country.
If there is one thing more than any other that will preserve private enterprise in this country it is the encouragement of industry to enter into retirement plans with a view to assuring a measure of security for their employees which too often in the past has been denied. As the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Gibson) has stated, many industries entered into this arrangement with a view to discharging their responsibilities to the end that private industry would not, at the expiry of the period of service on the part of their employees, place those employees out of work and a charge upon the country as a whole.
The annuity plan has been working out to the advantage of thousands and thousands of people who are under these employer-employee contracts. Without any warning, and indeed, without any justification, a decision was made which I do not believe represents the views of the minister and his department. We do not know why that change was made. We do not know who suggested it.
A commission was set up some years ago under the chairmanship of Mr. Justice Ives,
a former chief justice of Alberta, to inquire into the taxation of annuities. It found that eighty-seven per cent of the recipients of annuities held contracts for less than $900 a year, and that three-quarters of the annuitants were receiving less than $600 a year. It is something that benefited men and women with low incomes; it was not taken out to any extent by those with large incomes. According to the findings of the commission only 131 annuitants, or less than one-half of one per cent, were drawing over $1,200 a year, to which figure the amount of individual annuities was restricted in 1931.
In my opinion the action taken by this government constitutes a backward and improper step. The situation was summarized by the financial editor of one of the great newspapers in this country, who said:
. . . the change will sound the deathknell for a number of industrial pension plans now in the process of being set up.	.
One of the arguments used over and over again against private enterprise is that employers in business fail to assure the measure of security that they ought to for their employees. Because of the rates that were available and because the contracts they entered into were with the government, many employers entered into such contracts believing that the government would continue similar provisions in all future contracts. Even yet the minister should give reconsideration to the decision made by the order in council of April 19. Some reforms and changes should be made in the provisions of annuities; but to interfere with the principles of contracts is a denial of principle which cannot be denied.
I realize that it is almost useless to protest against what has been done, but I want the house and the country to know that in my opinion the action taken by the government was unjustifiable and should not be accepted by parliament.
Mr. ANGUS MaeINNIS (Vancouver East): Mr. Speaker, I want to say a few words on the second reading of this bill. The case against it was put most excellently by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles). The purpose of the annuities act when it was put on the statute books forty years ago was to help people with small means to save for the time when they would no longer be able to earn. We should not overlook that purpose.
We are now paying old age pensions to many people who are over the age of seventy years, and there is a growing demand that we begin paying these pensions at the age of sixty-five years. According to the statement given the
Government Annuities Act

other evening by the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin), we know there are now 275,000 persons receiving old age pensions. According to the figures given tonight by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, something over 210,000 are paying into the annuity plan.
Surely we should not place too much emphasis on the actuarial soundness of this scheme. The hon. member gave the deficit as being $1,500,000, including administration. If we take the number of persons paying into the scheme, this means about S7 a year per person. Surely it is worth $7 a year per person to this government to encourage people to pay into a plan of this kind, so that when they reach the age of sixty-five years, or whatever the retirement age is, they will have sufficient to look after themselves and not have to come to the state for old age pensions.
I think it would pay the government-by government I mean the people of this country, because, after all, it is the people who must pay the deficit-to make up this deficit. This government is contributing to a number of old age pensions, some in whole and some in part.
The contributions made by the government in 1946-47 to the civil service superannuation fund amounted to $3,160,000. Let it be clearly understood that I am not objecting to that; but consider the comparatively small number for whose benefit that was paid in comparison with the number of those who are trying to put something aside through the purchase of a government annuity in order that they may have some independence in their old age. It may be said these civil servants are working for the government and, because of that, they have a claim on the government for assistance in building up a superannuation fund. But I say they are no more working for the government than the great mass of the Canadian people who are working on our farms, in our factories, in our mines and in the mills, or wherever they may be, producing the wealth of this country. The minister is not in the house at the moment, but I suggest to his parliamentary assistant and to such members of the government as are now present that they reconsider this bill in all its implications and suspend discussion on it, so that further consideration may be given either to withdrawing it or to amending it drastically.

maintopic: PROVISIONS AS TO ISSUE, CONVERSION AND, AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the bill before us decreases the rate of interest paid to annuitants and diminishes the benefits of an annuity bought under this government scheme. It is difficult to understand the policies of the present government in

these days. One might expect retreat from good social legislation by a reactionary government. One would expect such a step as this in days of decadence, but it is not the sort of thing one would expect from a Liberal government. Today the Canadian people realize that a government annuity within the reach of the average Canadian citizen is both good government and good business, and the people of Canada are expecting the government to move in that direction. Instead, we find that the government is placing these government annuities a little further beyond the reach of the average citizen. In other words, a government annuity costs more and the returns from it are less. It can mean only one thing. It means that fewer people will buy government annuities and get the benefit of an annuity in their old age from the Canadian government. If we could get twice or three times as many Canadians to subscribe to a government annuity fund and get its benefits, we would save at least that much in the amount we have to pay out in old age pensions.
It is good for the people of a country to feel that they are providing for themselves in their old age through a government annuity scheme. The tragedy of poverty overtaking people in their declining years is only too evident in Canada today. Instead of doing something to relieve that situation and making people happier and more contented, we find a Liberal government making these annuities less attractive; going in the wrong direction altogether by placing these annuities further out of the reach of the people of this country. I do not know why the government is retreating from this field. I do not know whether they favour private enterprise moving in to occupy it, but I know that some day the real cause will be exposed. We cannot do much more than protest against the step that is being taken here, and we shall continue to protest against it. I assure the government of this, that they are moving in the wrong direction.
Mr. HARRY R. JACKMAN (Rosedale): Mr. Speaker, I am greatly surprised that the government should bring forwar d this measure to make it much more difficult than it has been for Canadian citizens to make some provision for their old age. I should think, with the social conscience which has developed in this country within the last fifteen or twenty years, that wherever there was some evidence of self-help on the part of our people, the government would certainly not discourage that tendency but would rather encourage it, even though it might have cost $1,500,060 each year, so that our Canadian people might by

Government Annuities Act
their own provision look forward to having some financial resources in their old age.
This bill not only reduces the interest rate from four to three per cent, but it makes the mortality table more severe, so that the cost goes up against the annuitant. Administrative costs, which in the case of all social measures such as the family allowance and so forth, have been borne by the government, will now be saddled upon those who are trying to help themselves in a very modest way by providing an income of $1,200 or less per annum for themselves; and the bill increases the maximum annuity by $300, making it $1,500 altogether.
What is the true rate of interest on money? This government, by its managed economy, by the operation of the Bank of Canada, has forced interest rates down, not to four per cent but to three per cent, and in recent years even less than that. We all remember when government bonds sold to yield five per cent; and I can recall Ontario bonds, when the credit of the province was as good as that of the dominion, selling to yield six per cent. Has the minister told us what the average rate of interest on Canadian bonds has been during the last twenty to thirty years? No, he has not. He would probably have to say it was in excess of four per cent, which up to the moment has been the prevailing rate on government annuities. But now, through the government's own manipulation of credit, having forced the rate of interest on bonds down to three per cent, it seeks to apply that rate against our citizens who are trying in a very modest way to provide some financial resources for their old age.
But in addition to having forced the interest rate down, what kind of dollars is this government giving to the people of Canada who, during the last twenty or thirty years, have been paying their hard-earned money into this government annuity scheme? Certainly they are not the same kind of dollars that were paid in. The government has benefited because, through the drop in the value of the dollar, the government, which got paid in three bushels of wheat or in three hours of work, is now paying it back at the rate of two bushels of wheat or two hours of work. Where is the fair play in that? Where is the even break which the government should give to its own citizens who have the foresight to try to look after themselves. The government has gained a tremendous amount in actual dollars under this annuity scheme. The so-called monetary loss of SI.500.000 a year does not begin to offet the actual gain which the government has made because of the changed value of the dollar. You pay in when
the dollar is a hard dollar, and the government pays out when the dollar is worth half as much.
I should also like to point out that under our old age pension scheme such as it is today we have the means test, which is an abomination and which accounted for the loss of seats to a certain political group in the province of Ontario recently as much as any other one thing did. Certainly in my own riding, provincially speaking, it was without question one of the greatest factors, and no differentiation was made between the dominion government and the provincial government in regard to the contributions or the administration of old age pensions. The means test, I repeat,, is an abomination.
I cannot understand for a moment why a young person starting out in work, who never expects^ to get a very great deal, because of his position or his contribution to our society, should save, since he is little better off at the end than if he had spent all the money himself. The old age pension comes along, and if the pensioner has some capital that he has saved he will not, because of this means test, get the benefit of his own savings.
To come to annuities in relation to old age pensions, as long as this system obtains, if a person has any income he or she does not get the old age pension, and that is another channel through which the dominion government has to date, although I hope it will not benefit much longer, saved for itself a great deal of money.
It would be interesting to know on whose advice the government has seen fit to introduce _ this measure. Is it on the advice of certain interested parties in this country, or is it on the advice of its own financial advisers? I think it would be of extreme interest to the house, if the minister, or the parliamentary assistant in charge of the bill, would indicate to us just where the suggestion came from.
There are objections on the part of some institutions which sell annuities that it has been unfair to them for the government to quote lower rates, but I believe the social significance of government annuities far outweighs any objections which they might have.
It has also been pointed out that well-to-do people have taken advantage of the government annuities system whereby they can get four per cent interest on their savings rather than three per cent if they invested those savings directly in government bonds. But there are comparatively few people in that class who take advantage of it; and, as has been pointed
Government Annuities Act

out by one of my colleagues, the average annuity under the government scheme is for less than $600.
The bearing of this change upon the employee retirement plans will be of great significance. It has been an inducement for corporations to inaugurate retirement plans, using dominion government annuities as the basis, because there was at least some semblance of a fair return on contributions by employer and by employee when four per cent was allowed on them. It might be said that everyone does not share in these government annuities, and that is so. They are not universal, but they are open to all. Yet the government sees fit to discourage those who are willing to exercise some measure of self-help.
I cannot refrain at this moment from saying a word about the government's attitude, now as in past years, towards government annuities. It is only a matter of four or five years since the Liberal government caused Canada to break its word for, I believe, the first time on record, when, after having sold these annuities on the basis of a limitation of $1,200 per annum, which would be tax free, the government changed the method of taxation and subjected them to income tax. Subsequently seeing the wrongfulness of that action, they retraced their steps to some extent, and a new provision was passed whereby only the income-earning element and not the capital of the annuity was taxed. I think it is now on a fair basis; nevertheless the government has not wiped off the stain left on its escutcheon when it committed a breach of faith and broke the word of the dominion with people who had purchased the annuities.
May I also point out that when it is said that these annuities under the present four per cent rate are costing the taxpayer generally a certain amount of money, even though it is small, there are many things under our system as it obtains today wherein there is not complete fairness or equity. I shall mention the retirement plans which exist under many corporations and institutions, and even under the government itself.
There the worker is allowed to deduct, let us say four or five per cent of his wages and have the amount paid into the retirement plan before taxation, and in practically every case the corporation or employer will contribute a similar amount which does not enter into his taxation bracket. Ultimately, when the employee benefits, when he is retired, the amount he gets is taxed, but it is obvious to all that at that time the former employee's income bracket is such that he is subject to little or no tax. Yet the great bulk of our

citizens are not fortuniate enough to belong to institutions, whether the government or large corporations, that can afford to put into operation these retirement plans, so that they cannot save before taxation as can hundreds of thousands of our citizens who do come under these retirement plans which get the authorization of the Minister of Finance.
So there we have one continuing form of discrimination, if the government wishes tu rely on discrimination as the basis for making this change in government annuities. I believe, and certainly the Progressive Conservative party believes, that we should make adequate provision for the old age of our people, and we believe that it should be made under a contributory old age pension scheme.
When a young man or a young woman starts working, he or she should start contributions to a plan; the employer should make a contribution, and the state should make a contribution, so that when that young man or young woman reaches the age of retirement, he or she can retire with a competence which is at least decent and not insufficient to keep body and soul together.
I believe it is an essential lack of sincerity in any party which believes in a contributory old age pension plan if it feels that it can support this bill, which makes it more difficult for our people to provide a reasonable measure of social security for themselves. Certainly I for one believe, in fact I not only believe but I think I may say I know, that with the resources and the prosperity of the country we must put a floor of social security under our people.
This government, however, in introducing this change in the annuities act, is making it more difficult for the individual to put a floor under himself. So that the government is not living up to what might be considered its declared principles, and certainly the Progressive Conservative party believes in a contributory old age pension scheme in which there will be a contribution by the state. The amount that is now given by the government under the dominion annuities scheme is a very small contribution. We must have a floor of social security under our people, and we must keep the gates of opportunity open, so that above that floor there will not be a limit which will discourage the best efforts oi our people.

speechtext: Order. I must ask bon. members to moderate their voices. It is difficult to hear the hon. member who is speaking.

Having gone over with some care what the minister has said with respect to his general policy, I am happy to be able to express approval of his general outlook, attitude and aim as he has expressed it. He realizes that one of the serious problems confronting the country at the present time is the shortage of United States dollars; and he is undoubtedly seeking to organize the economy of Canada in such a way as to safeguard her against too serious difficulties arising out of that condition. But I believe the minister will have to adopt measures, or at least that he will have to cause the government to adopt measures which are not implied in anything which he has said up to the present time.
I should like to talk for a short time about this United States dollar shortage. It seems to me that not enough attention is being given to it in a general way. The United States dollar shortage is not something new. It is not a postwar phenomenon. It is not a temporary or passing ailment which the world *can sleep off, work off, outgrow or, by natural means, recover from. The United States dollar shortage is rather a malignant malady, like pernicious anaemia, diabetes or rheumatoid arthritis, developing from deep-seated, fundamental, organic causes. If we are to cope successfully with this United States dollar shortage we must seek out those causes and remove, cure or counteract them.
When did the shortage of United States dollars become a reality? I find the general impression to be that the United States dollar shortage is something resulting from the recently finished war. But such is not the case. The United States dollar shortage began to develop right after 1919 when the United States became a creditor nation with high tariff protection. It became pronounced by 1926 and continued so through 1929.
I think a word or two of comment is desirable at this point. Great Britain was a creditor nation for a number of years, but you never
heard of a shortage of British pounds. Why was it that all through the one hundred years preceding world war I you never heard of a shortage of British pounds, while immediately the United States becomes a creditor nation you begin to hear about a shortage of United States dollars? Why was that? The fundamental reason was that when Britain was a creditor nation she always accepted goods from abroad in payment for her own goods. But when the United States became a creditor nation she refused to accept goods from abroad in payment for the goods she sold. This is one of the fundamental facts that it is necessary to keep in mind in order to comprehend the general situation in which we find ourselves.
I would say that the shortage of United States dollars developed immediately after 1919, just as soon as the United States became a creditor nation. From 1919 through 1929 the United States provided by loan some $7,500 million of new capital to other countries, more than the total of similar issues floated in the United Kingdom, France, The Netherlands and all other capital-lending countries combined. In the nineteen-thirties such loans came to a complete standstill, while a heavy net inflow of capital came into the United States from other countries. Hon. members will find this matter scientifically, interestingly and authentically discussed on page 31 of "The United States in World Economy," a book in the library of parliament. Again, more than $900 million a year had to be paid to the United States by other nations as fixed debt service obligations of those nations to the United States resulting from world war I and from United States foreign investments or loans abroad. Hon. members will find this also discussed in "The United States in World Economy" at page 31.
United States tourists spent abroad more than $6 billion between 1918 and 1939, and only slightly below $500 million in 1929. This is also well discussed in "The United States in World Economy" at page 75. But these tourists' expenditures almost completely ceased after 1929. The reason why it is wise to discuss the matters which I am now discussing is that we are likely to see a repetition of these things which occurred in the United States between world war I and world war II. If we are to have ourselves strong enough and well enough cushioned to resist successfully the impact of untoward conditions in the United States we shall have to govern ourselves with extreme wisdom and vision.
How serious is this United States situation at the present time? The United States normally sells the world $12 billion worth of goods more than she buys from the world a year.

May I repeat, that the solution lies along the line of imperial preferences and the sterling system of interstate finance for British commonwealth and empire countries. Another development is a modification of the sterling system, which I believe is the one best adapted to save the situation for the world.
In respect, of an international distribution of goods, the proposal has been made that the sterling system of international state finance be modified and extended into something like the system of contra account which is suggested by the London chamber of commerce in its report of September 30, 1947. What does this contra account mean? It practically means this in a general way: If the United States were selling a vast amount of goods to the world, as she is, she would say to the nations of the world: We will let you have $12,000,000 more of goods than you can let us have, and we will allow you credit for these goods as long as you are unable to produce and repay us with goods, and then, just as soon as you have goods to send back to us in return, we will accept them. That is to say, we are selling you the goods on a lend-lease basis of credit, and we shall expect back from the nations of the world such goods as they are able to supply us with. That would be, in a way a system of contra account. This method or some modification of it we shall have to adopt if we1 are to get ourselves out of the dangerous situation in which we find ourselves.

This is possibly one of the most important departments of the government. I have listened with considerable interest to the hon. member who has just taken his seat, and I cannot help but feel that experience is indeed a great teacher. One of the problems we are suffering from today is an over-expansion of credit and currency, and I often wonder, as I listen to my hon. friend and his colleagues, just how they can

Supply-Trade and Commerce
reconcile their position today with their professed desire in the past to pay out dividends to the citizens of Alberta on a basis of S25 a month. If such a policy were in force today it could but increase the pressure against prices.
As a student of monetary reform and as one who believes that there is much room for improvement in our present monetary system, I have always held to the view that only a dollar earned is a dollar that has any value. You cannot get something for nothing. But it seems to me that the system advocated by my hon. friend and his colleagues is based on providing something for nothing.
Would my hon. friend permit a question?	.
So long as you do not attempt to continue your speech.

It is just a question. Will my hon. friend devote his attention to the subject I discussed tonight. I did not mention money or dividends at all. If he wants to discuss monetary reform I shall be glad to discuss it with him, but he had better come well prepared. I was discussing tonight the world problem of distribution.

In order that there may be no misunderstanding, may I say that I hold my hon. friend in the very highest regard. We differ in our opinions, and I was simply reminding him of one of the weaknesses of their program. I like people with ideas; I think they did have an idea which they tried to sell and certainly, in days gone by, in the hungry thirties a shot in the arm would have been good for this nation. I am concerned, however, about the immediate present, and I feel that we are too closely tied with the United States. As a matter of fact, there is great danger of our becoming an economic adjunct of that great republic. They are admirable as friends, but the Americans are pretty hard, cold-blooded dealers. They are two-fisted in their approach to commercial problems, and I regret to find that our whole future is more or less predicated upon the success of the Marshall plan or some plan that is evolved in the United States.
I suggest that, with Canada's great resources, we should stand on our own feet and plan accordingly. We have every reason to determine our own future course, and it would be well to strengthen our position in relation to the British preferential pacts within the sterling bloc. It is perhaps unfortuate that we are one of those countries in the dollar bloc, so closely related to the dollar countries. History reveals that, in the past, three-fifths of the world's commerce and trade took place within the sterling bloc; these two great blocs
are now pitted against each other, and we find ourselves in the dollar block.
Is it not most unfortunate that when we were in such a really enviable position we cast it away? It is not long since that Canada had a 90-cent dollar. Bretton Woods had been presented to the house, together with the terms of the international bank. We knew then that we were required to value our currency at the rate of exchange prevailing at the time we entered Bretton Woods. We could not depreciate our currency more than ten per cent without the consent >of that international organization, and yet, on the very eve of our entry into Bretton Woods, this government found it convenient, for reasons that I shall never understand, to bring our dollar up to parity with that of the United States. They robbed us of the most enviable position we shall ever have enjoyed in the realm of trade and commerce, because, as long as the United States dollar was accepted as the standard of exchange, we had access to the markets of the world.
Latin America lay open to our enterprise, open to our commerce and our trade, and likewise the countries of Europe enjoying a ten per cent advantage in the Canadian market. We were bound to reach those centres where our goods could be marketed and sold, which are at present denied to us because we have put an artificial prop under our Canadian dollar.
I say, Mr. Chairman, and I think I can discuss the question with some degree of authority, that the moment you put an artificial prop under the dollar, you interfere with the very lifeblood of a nation's trade and commerce. It naturally follows that the dollar should have been allowed to seek its own level in the world's markets, which, of course, there has been some effort to regulate and control. I am not denying that there should be some regulation, but we enjoyed a preferred position as our goods flowed over our borders into distant parts of the world where they were required and desired; and if our dollar had been allowed to seek its own level, by and by, of its own volition, it would have levelled itself with the United States dollar.
But we sought to place a handicap on the Canadian trader and producer, in spite of the fact that our production during the war was sufficient to stagger the human imagination. Indeed, the productive capacity of Canada is unlimited, and when I read in the press items advertising "Canada unlimited" I subscribe entirely to the theory. But we sought to place a handicap on our traders by saying to them, "You must meet the competition of one of the greatest producing nations in the world,
Supply-Trade and, Commerce

the United States, that have not only the productive capacity but the wealth of resources to stimulate that production and maintain their standard of living at a level comparable with Canada's". I am not one of those who say our standard of living is lower than theirs.
Canada, nevertheless, is going to pay a great price, because not only are we losing the present market but we are losing the potential market of the future. Had Canada's goods been flowing into Latin American countries and into other parts of the world we would have established a name for this dominion. The label "Canada" would have been known far and wide and people would have sought to place return orders. The Minister of Trade and Commerce is seeking to stimulate trade, and through his own good offices and the offices of those associated with him, he arranged the world trade conference, or show or exhibition in Toronto.
This government has always professed a belief in greater freedom of trade and exchange. I listened at home to the admirable words of the Prime Minister speaking from Europe when he announced the introduction of the Geneva trade pacts, and that was indeed a step in the direction of greater and freer world trade. But the radio suddenly switched from one program to the other, and the Minister of Finance made his announcement setting up artificial barriers in our own country and placing the obstacle of a 25 per cent excise tax in the way of the production of goods in this dominion.
The government tried to prove to the outside world that our dollar is as good as the United States dollar. We do not wish to be proud of these things, because if your dollar depreciates you have a trading advantage. I would point out, however, that the suggestion that our dollar was worth a dollar in the United States was after all only a joke, because it has been discounted right along, as high as from ten to fifteen per cent even in the border city of Buffalo; and while they endeavoured to prove that our dollar was worth a dollar in the United States they said to the Canadian people that it was worth only seventy-five cents at home, because they put a 25 per cent excise tax upon it.
I am one of those who had much to do with war savings certificates, and I am proud of my contribution in the way of encouraging our people to invest in them. The little $4 certificate was redeemable in seven and a half years at So. It was said to be the only government bond in the world which bore interest at 3J per cent, compounded semi-annually. In other words, in seven and a half years it returned $5 for $4 invested. There was also

a limit on the amount that one could invest- $480 a year or $40 a month-but at the end of seven and a half years one received back 850 a month.
There are some things I have to answer for myself, not because I have been a follower of the administration, but rather because I believed in their sincerity at the time; but now we find that, while these people are having $5 returned to them for $4 they invested, there is an excise tax of 25 per cent imposed upon their savings, and the dollar is worth only sixty-five cents.
I think the Minister of Trade and Commerce has a great deal of influence with the government-he has managed most of the departments-and my plea is that we be allowed to have an honest dollar. Let us do something to stimulate the productive capacity of the country. Let us remove this doubt and confusion. Today we find our gold mines languishing; and many of our natural resources which could be more properly developed are being neglected, all because of government regulation, bureaucratic control, an army of civil servants going across the land to determine whether a gold producing property is entitled to a bonus. Everything is done to hamper trade rather than to stimulate it.
The taxpayers of Canada are paying a terrific price. We know now there was no thought on the part of this government to reduce taxation, which would have lent the greatest stimulus to production that could possibly have been given to the Canadian people. With the huge surplus of upwards of $700 million, the government failed to bring any relief to the over-burdened taxpayers of Canada, but rather was satisfied to see them remain under the handicap which is of the governments' own making. I say that with every degree of sincerity, advisedly and wholeheartedly, because I am firmly of the opinion that the more you interfere with natural laws, the more difficult will it be to govern.
I say this to the government. If you want to join with my hon. friends on my left and drive this country into a state of socialism where there will be controls and greater controls, then you are in a fair way to bring about that very result. But if you want to encourage and develop the greatest degree of enterprise, enthusiasm, ambition, loyalty and determination in order to see this country through to its greatest destiny, you will encourage private enterprise to play its full part in the onward march of civilization. Not only do there lie before us green fields which look good a long way off; but we have back of us the resources and the productive capacity as well as the enthusiasm, initiative and

Let us indeed join with the British commonwealth. Let us determine, as we did in those dark days of the war, that we will stand by Britain and see her through; that we will not become an adjunct of the United States of America, either politically or economically ; and that we will stand on our own and develop our own resources to our greatest capacity.
