Why talk that way? That is no answer at all.
The same answer as you got.

We are entitled to know in this House of Commons from the Minister of Trade and Commerce what the position is with regard to the preference between Canada and the nations of the commonwealth, other than the United Kingdom. If the minister cannot give ui! that information tonight, then I sug-gnel thal the item be allowed to stand until he can get if. Does the minister refuse to get the information?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: Refuse to get it?
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: It is not in my department.
Well, where can you get it, then?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: Get it from the tariff board or the Minister of Finance.

That shows once more the minister's utter failure to appreciate the type of parliament by which this country is supposed to be governed. Here he is, taking a stand in a Canadian parliament, that if information is wanted with regard to a trade agreement parliament must go and ask the tariff board. That shows his utter contempt for our parliamentary system. If the rest of the members are satisfied with it, I certainly am not. It is a strange position indeed at which we have arrived when a minister of the crown, the one who has the responsibility at this time for most of the business being done by the government, can take that stand in the house, and just say, "Oh, well, it is not up to me to give the information. You just run along and get it from the tariff board, or from somebody else". I suggest to you, Mr. Chairman, that parliamentary government has reached a sorry stage in Canada when that is the type of answer given by a minister of the crown.

I should like to ask the
minister a question, in a kindly way. I have been away from the house for some time, and perhaps I am not in touch with all that has taken place. The day before leaving, I mentioned the matter of fish livers going across to the United States, wdiere there used to be an embargo. The people out west who process by far the greater portion of these fish livers- I refer to the co-operative-are still interested in the matter. I am sure this comes under the minister's jurisdiction, because it was through his department that the embargo was lifted. Has there been any change in policy, or does the minister contemplate any change? There is still a ten per cent duty on processed oils going into the United States. The government would not be embarrassing itself under the Geneva trade agreements by its commitments respecting oils from the Pacific coast. I do not refer to the east coast, because that is a different set of conditions altogether. That was explained, to me.
There is a ten per cent tariff on processed oils, and I want to know if the government intends to reimpose the embargo to protect the industry which has been built up on the Pacific coast.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext:
Here again the Department of
Trade and Commerce acts on the advice of the Minister of Fisheries. It is all very well to put embargoes on to prevent trade from going across the line, except in finished form. That is a very fine protectionist theory; but it is not very good for the producer. I suppose

Supply-Trade and Commerce
the man who catches the fish and extracts the liver would not give three cheers for a policy which would prevent his shipping his product across the line, if he wished to do so.
However, the whole matter has been studied by the Minister of Fisheries, and a decision has been made. I am not sure what the decision is, but I shall endeavour to find out and tell the hon. member.
The Minister of Fisheries is right behind you.

If the minister's department has no control over tariffs and trade, I am wondering why his predecessor took such an extended tour of South America and empire countries, for the purposes, we believed, to build up empire trade. It seems strange to me that tonight the minister should deny his jurisdiction in these matters, or deny having any influence.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: The answer to that is quite obvious. The minister did not go to South Africa to make a trade treaty. I might say his trip was very successful, because we are doing an enormous amount of trade with South Africa. Much of that was arranged during the course of that expedition. If my hon. friend wishes to talk about trade, and not trade treaties, I will talk with him as long as he likes.

Mr. Chairman, surely the minister will not take the position that we cannot properly ask him, the Minister of Trade and Commerce, about the state of treaties on which our trade depends-'the state of treaties between this country and other parts of the commonwealth. I cannot believe the minister would take that position. It does not seem reasonable.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: If my hon. friend will talk about treaties where trade is flowing, we can give the answers. If he is talking about treaties where no trade is flowing, it is difficult to give the answer, because we are not very much interested in them.
Perhaps it would be better if you were, probably there would be more trade. But, speaking seriously, surely what the hon. member for Vancouver South asked was quite reasonable.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: His question was a political one. If I knew the answer I would give it to him.

It was not a political
question.
Now we are coming to it.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: He is just back from the hustings, you know.
So are you; that would explain it. But this is a direct question to which I think the hon. member is entitled to an answer.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: I do not know the answer.
Find it then.

Get it. Surely it is not unreasonable-and I want to ask my own question, too. But I put it to the minister that he is not going to leave it in that way, and that he will get the information-because it is reasonable.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: I have the answer now. There was a modification with the United Kingdom. With Australia and New Zealand and South Africa there was no modification.
No modification?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: No.

The minister made a statement the other night, which appeared at page 5070 of Hansard, wherein he gave the figures of monthly imports under schedule III. In the items there, I notice a large drop in the first group, covering motorcars, and quite a large percentage drop in film projectors, although that was a relatively small item. Then, with regard to subsequent groups of items, there is very little drop; in fact, in the last group there is an actual increase. What is the policy under this item, particularly with regard to the last two groups where there is little or no reduction. It will be noted that in the fourth group there is an increase from 1947.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: Is the hon. member referring to table II or table III?
Table II.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: I am not sure of the point my hon. friend is trying to make. He will observe that the controls came into force for different items at different dates. In connection with the items in that table, some controls came into effect only on April 1, 1948. That is group 4. Is that the one the hon. member is referring to?
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext:
The reason there is very little effect is that during the period covered by the table the controls were not in force.
Supply-Trade and Commerce

Except for the month of April. I see the minister's point. With regard to the third group, the controls came into effect in March. Does the minister expect that there will be in these items anything like the reduction there has been in the first group, or are these items where his policy will be to allow the situation to run along pretty well as it is?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: There is not the same potential for saving as there- is in the first group. Those items are not made in the same volume, but the same policies will apply and I think there will be the same proportion of savings.
With regard to fabricated steel and so on?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext:
That is in a little different position. This is a deficit country as far as steel is concerned. We manufacture about 3,000,000 tons, but we have to import 1,000,000 tons a year and Canadian industry depends upon that importation very heavily. For instance, our motor industry could not operate at all without a good deal of imported sheet. We just have not the capacity to make it here. There is hardly a heavy industry in the country that does not depend to some extent on imported steel. As far as the construction industry is concerned, all the larger structural shapes are imported.
We have hesitated to apply controls to these steel items because of a fear of retaliation, speaking frankly. It would take some persuasion to have the steel mills give us the sheet we require, because they would take the position, "If you do not want structural, you cannot get sheet." Therefore, we have not applied controls to those items for that reason.
How much would that be effective if our construction turned from large factory construction and such to small dwellings? Would that affect our import requirements of steel?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: We would use less structural steel, because there is nothing that I would call structural steel in a house. However, there is a great deal of structural steel used in a hydroelectric plant and in other types of construction that contribute directly to the economic strength of this country. My hon. friend knows we are short of hydroelectric power, and hydroelectric plants have the highest priorities.

As the minister knows, before the war our trading situation depended upon what was called the Atlantic triangle; that is, trade between the United States, Great Britain and Canada was pretty well balanced out. Is

it thought that this position will again prevail or must we plan on the inability to re-establish that position?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: The triangle is working now up to a degree. The breakdown in the triangle is due to the United Kingdom not being in a position to ship goods in the volume they did formerly. It is working as far as it can work. One of the principal purposes of the European recovery program is to build up the productive strength of Britain to the point where the triangle can work fully. It is not working fully at this time; it is working to a small extent and a little better each month, I am happy to say. There is nothing much we can do about it except to try to make it work.
Is it believed that the plan will work again fully in the course of time, or must we provide some new plan for our Canadian trade?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: It is difficult to say. We sincerely hope it will, and all our efforts are being directed toward the restoring of the triangle in full. I will not venture to predict whether we can do it, and I do not think anyone else would. Our trade figures are better each month and Britain's position is improving _ each month, but the operation of the triangle depends upon the ability of Britain to export more than they import, and today they are importing far more than they are exporting.
Our plan is based on the eventual return of the triangle?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: We are trying to develop multilateral trade. We trade where we can trade, and we shall always be in that position. But we are doing all we can to bulid up the economic strength of Britain so that the triangle can work.
Is Britain getting her imports from Canada on the quota basis today as she did a year or so ago?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: Is my hon. friend referring to token imports?
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: There has been no change.
Does your department have something to say in regard to how they shall work?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext:
Yes, that is correct. Of course we do not decide what the token imports will be. We negotiate with Britain to get a list of token imports, and after that we have something to say. We issue the certificates, but more or less as agents for the United Kingdom.

Supply-Trade and Commerce
You select the company or the firm that ships the goods?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: No. The firms make their sales in the United Kingdom, but we issue the export permits more or less as the United Kingdom asks us to.

What are the conditions underlying imports from Britain? Is it their capacity to manufacture goods, or is it price and tariff conditions here? We did make a special tariff adjustment to facilitate the import of certain rayon goods. Will the minister say what the limiting factor is, because the figures are still disappointing, or at any rate they are quite small.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: A larger proportion of Britain's over-all exports are coming to Canada each month than previously, but there is some difficulty about price. Some goods are over-priced. We have done our best to correct that situation; we have removed the dump against certain British goods and are doing all we can to help Britain sell goods here at prices that our people are willing to pay. The great difficulty is that Britain has not the goods to ship in the volume we would like to receive.

I met a British industrialist a few days ago, and I got the impression from him that it was partly a question of more favourable selling conditions elsewhere. I suppose that that is always relatively true. Is there a definite advantage to the British to sell in sterling countries as against us? Are they more in balance? As we turn, as I suppose we shall to some extent, to a buyers' market and not a sellers' market, will the difficulty of their selling goods increase?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: I always understood that Britain had a full-out campaign to exchange goods for dollars. I think at the moment the pressure is 'behind the export of goods to dollar countries. It is easier for Britain to trade with sterling countries because they use a common currency.

Are not Britain's trade difficulties with Canada twofold? The main difficulty is, I think, her shortage of goods that Canada wants. If she can increase her production of the kind of goods that Canada will buy she can increase her trade with Canada greatly if Canada will buy those goods, but unless we are willing to buy them there is not much prospect of a great increase in her trade with us.

Under which minister does the issuing of permits under schedule 1 come? Is it the Minister of Trade and 5849-344J
Commerce, the Minister of Finance or some other minister? If it is the Minister of Trade and Commerce I would ask him whether permits have been issued for the importation of any of these articles in schedule 1 from Great Britain. I know that sweet biscuits are coming in.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: The Minister of Finance administers schedule 1 and schedule 2 of the act, and the Minister of Trade and Commerce administers schedule 3. I have no knowledge of what has come in under schedule 1.

It surely comes within the minister's purview to have something to do with the promotion of trade, and surely he has something to do with the endeavour to make Canada self-sufficient, particularly in regard to products which we ordinarily purchase from the United States. But I find from the trade returns that in the first three months of 1947 Canada imported muskrat skins from the United States to the value of $1,783,000, and in the first three months of 1948', $2,824,000 worth, or an increase of over $1,000,000 worth. Under the embargo measure, no fresh lettuce is coming in this year, but in the first three months of last year we imported $993,000 worth from the United States. Of rabbit skins, undressed, we imported $153,000 in the first three months of 1947, and $781,450 in the first three months of 1948. Cannot we raise muskrats in Canada? Will rabbits not breed in Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: The fur trade is complicated. Fur auctions are held in St. Louis, and many of our furs are bought there. Rabbit skins practically all come from Australia, but they come to Canada through the United States. We are not producers of rabbit skins, but we are producers of the most expensive fur-such as fox and beaver. On balance, we are heavy exporters of skins, and if we were to take measures to exclude small imports from other countries it might have a detrimental effect on our export trade.
Can we not encourage the breeding of muskrats in this country? Are any United States funds involved in purchasing these rabbit skins from Australia which come in through the United States?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext:
These international currencies move around. I presume the Americans get some little rake-off on the skins as they pass through the United States. We buy our Australian rabbit skins from the market in St. Louis, I am told. I presume that the Australians get United States dollars from the United States and send them over to us to
Supply-Trade and Commerce

buy lumber. I could not say that the Americans do not get some dollars out of that transaction.

I understand that there is a fur auction in Montreal. The minister is interested in developing trade, particularly with the other parts of the commonwealth. Why is something not done by way of getting these Australian rabbit skins shipped direct to Canada, without having to go through the United States, where a certain amount of commission must be paid?

The minister knows that one of our troubles in getting goods from Britain is the high price of those goods. The U.S.A. World- News Report points out that that is one of the main difficulties. They say that British textiles are piling up on the shelves in Britain, because they cannot be sold on account of their high prices. You could buy English shirts in Ottawa in 1939 for $3, and a year ago you could buy them for $6.50, but last fall they cost $9. The minister mentioned that we have eliminated the tariff to help Britain. I went downtown this week expecting to find some slight reduction, but I iound that English shirts bad gone up fifty [DOT]cents to $9.50. Why should the price of these articles go up when we have eliminated the tariff? Has the price level of British goods gone up recently, or are these prices due to .action on the part of retailers in this country?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: It is difficult to say. If my hon. friend is shocked by those prices I can tell him that I bought some shirts the last time I was in Britain and I was shocked to find that the bill came to $20 per shirt. You can buy British shirts cheaper in Canada than in Britain. I cannot say whether the prices are going up or not. Our dealers in British goods are anxious to reintroduce these goods and their mark-up should be very modest. It is difficult to say, without investigating the particular commodity.

It is nearly eleven o'clock and, when we resume, I should like the minister to give us a statement on the total credits we have given to date to facilitate our trade. Just where do we stand at the moment?
Item stands.
Progress reported.

speakerposition: topic

speechtext: May I ask the Minister of Finance when he proposes to bring in the income tax bill for discussion?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The one that is being considered by the banking and commerce committee? I hope early next week.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Tomorrow we
shall take up the resolution in the name of the Prime Minister, concerning the increase in salary of the lieutenant governor of Prince Edward Island, and we hope we shall pass the resolution and the bill in its different stages. The bill is exactly the same as the resolution. It is to increase the salary from $7,000 to $8,000. Then we shall consider amendments made by the senate to Bill No. 228 and Bill No. 300; then take up Bill No. 349, to amend the Diplomatic Service Superannuation Act. Then we shall go into supply, taking the estimates of trade and commerce, reconstruction, veterans affairs, external affairs, labour, national revenue, public works. I cannot indicate in what order we shall take them up.
